text: First of all, the first gameplay experience is unmatched. The world is insanely beautiful, the characters are memorable, and the voice acting is perfect. Every line feels heavy and meaningful. The dialogues hit hard...you can feel the weight behind them.  About the Difficulty :  The game’s difficulty depends entirely on how you choose to play. Yes, skill matters...but even a noob like me can finish this game.  If you decide to fight bosses without summons or without some broken one-shot build, the game becomes hard as hell. You’re forced to rely purely on skill. Summons, on the other hand, make the game much easier.  For me, Mimic Tear carried my entire playthrough, even against Malenia, and I was using a pretty random build to be honest. For some reason, Mimic Tear didn’t help much in the Radagon fight...but Tiche absolutely did.  I personally don’t want to spend hours fighting a single boss. My first playthrough took 94 hours, and even with Mimic Tear helping me, it already took a long time. Without Mimic Tear, it would’ve taken me way more than that...there’s honestly no way I could’ve completed the game. That said, there is one thing that genuinely made the game harder for me...and I’ll explain that in the “What I Hate” section.  What I Loved About the Game :  The beautiful environment goes without saying, but exploration is the real star of Elden Ring.  This is the only game where I explored this much. I’ve never explored any other game the way I explored this one...not even Red Dead Redemption 2 or The Witcher 3, where exploration is also a huge focus. Everywhere you go, something is waiting for you...a boss, a weapon, a Somber Smithing Stone, or even something you didn’t know you needed.  Even when I found items I wasn’t interested in, it still felt satisfying. Exploration never felt wasted. Even after exploring for hours, I still feel like there are so many things left to discover.  Honestly, 60–70% of my playtime was just exploration, not boss fights ...and I loved every second of it.  One more thing I absolutely loved was weapons, especially my favorite one.. the Uchigatana with the Unsheathe skill. I honestly can’t explain how satisfying that weapon feels. I used the Uchigatana for almost every boss in the game, right up until I found Rivers of Blood. The Unsheathe skill just hits different.  I know the Uchigatana isn’t really a late-game weapon...at least not with the skillset I have...but it’s still my favorite weapon in the game, no lie.  As for the story… I’ll be honest I barely understood anything except “Put these foolish ambitions to rest.” I’ll definitely watch lore videos later. I’m just bad at grasping stories when the narration isn’t direct. But I’m sure it won’t disappoint.  Boss designs and movesets are also fantastic.  What I Hated About the Game :  This is purely my opinion nd you don’t have to agree.  The combat. I don’t enjoy dodging 3–4 attacks just to land one hit or only to get interrupted or staggered while using a skill attack. Many weapons have amazing movesets, but the real question is ...can we actually use them effectively? I’m not so sure. Maybe skill issue from my side ..but srsly.  Another thing I hated was how the dodge  works.  Dodging doesn’t always respond instantly if you’re already attacking or stuck at the end of an animation and that often gets you hit. My first Soulslike game was Black Myth Wukong, where dodging is instant. No matter what you’re doing...if you press dodge, you dodge.  That’s why combat in BMW feels so much better and more satisfying to me than in Elden Ring.  That’s exactly how I wanted Elden Ring’s dodge to feel. If dodging worked like that, half the game would instantly feel easier. And that’s why BMW felt much easier to me compared to Elden Ring. If instant dodge were removed from BMW, it wouldn’t be any easier than Elden Ring at all.  This is honestly the only major thing I hated about the game.  Final Verdict :  Despite my complaints, I absolutely loved exploring this world, and overall, I enjoyed the game a lot.  I’ll still say it straight: Elden Ring is a 10/10. You won’t regret buying this game and giving it a shot.

text: Sharing my thoughts because while looking through reviews it seemed like I was in an echo chamber without criticism. While impressive for an early access game, I feel as if this game has a while to go until I can recommend this game as a sequel to Hades. The new combat system was interesting at first but the more you play it the more you realize how much it slows the combat down and it becomes a slog. Weapon animations feel sluggish and movement has been completely gutted. We traded multiple dashes for a sprint mechanic that doesn't feel amazing and further slows down the gameplay. I understand that Super Giant is approaching this game with a different combat system in mind, but it seems that they've only taken away things that made the previous game amazing without adding anything noteworthy to compensate. Boons feel weak, non-impactful, and all around samey. Progression feels all over the place, one moment you have no upgrades, and the next moment you're upgrading 4 things at once.   Let me be clear here, I'm not posting this just to trash on the game or hoping for its downfall. I wish the best for this game because I truly love it and see how much love was put into this game. Everything outside of what I pointed out is beautiful, be it the story, art, music, or voice acting. Everything. I want this game to become the best it could be and will gladly change my review once the game is further updated and refined. text: TLDR: If you're particularly unskilled.  Hades II really took a lot of tools away, and it really doesn't want you to clear it.  Or it wants you to spend many, many runs grinding for advantages.  Yes, this game is recommended for MOST players.  It has great music and dialogue.  It's beautiful, and has a lot of bold build decisions over Hades.  Weapons definitely take longer to figure out.  HOWEVER.  The game is not for everyone.  The game is designed defensively, as though Supergiant games was upset about how fast people progressed through Hades.  Runs take longer.  Bosses have more invincibility phases.  Everything takes longer to unlock.  They've diversified resources and given you two options about what you do each run, which is cool!  Strangely, the layers are actually EASIER with only a couple bosses being a problem, but what a problem they are....  Hades II has a slightly lower rating than Hades, and I suspect that's never going to change.  They made the game harder.  They made death defiance MUCH harder to get.  The final boss is tremendously harder than Hades.  They took out multiple dashes.  The game tried to "fix" how "easily" people could get through it, and I think the difference in positive reviews are just the people who've been left behind.  I'm middle aged, blind, and very slow.  Double dashes producing buckets of i-frames were pretty much the only way I could keep progressing in Hades.  I've fought Chronos eight or nine times.  I no longer think I can beat him.  His tells are very hard to read.  The models in this game are very small, and he's a gold figure on a gold background.  He's ALSO very fast.  Even if I wanted to do God Mode I'd be looking at a dozen or so runs before the bonuses stacked up enough for me to kill him.  The whole time the run up to him would be getting duller and duller and duller....  I give the game a good rating, because it is excellent in so much of what it does.  I just wanted to point out that it has left people behind.  It's harder, grindier, and takes away strategies that the unskilled used to compensate.  But statistically, you are younger and better at games.  You should definitely pick this up.  It's a real gem.

text: It honestly pains me to have to write a bad review for Hades 2. I've been playing since the warsong update and from the beginning I fell in love with this game. It had a captivating storyline, lush and stunning visuals, a fantastic soundtrack, a lovable, compelling, beautifully voiced cast of characters that I instantly got attached to, and I found the gameplay ten times more fun, smooth, and satisfying than the first.  I adored Hades 2. I recommended it to anyone that would listen, defended it from criticism, and eagerly lapped up all new content. I was over the moon when 1.0 was announced and counted down the days to the full release.   And then I saw the ending.  What the fuck, Supergiant!?   I don't even know where to begin with this. every single plot point I was interested in lead to nothing. Every character I liked got bastardized to Tartarus and back. All the build-up, all the anticipation, leads up to one of the worst video game endings I have possibly ever seen. I kept thinking "Okay, it can't possibly get worse than this" and then it did.  Melinoe is the worst victim of the character assassination, which was incredibly disappointing as I found her a very likeable protagonist, and one of my favourite characters in the cast. All her motivation, ambition, and personality is thrown away for a cheap "feel good" power of friendship ending that completely ignores her struggles and character arc. text: [h2]P.S. THIS WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS FOR THE ENDING.[/h2]  [b]P.P.S. Supergiant has reworked the ending from its previous four-car pileup to a more gentle, screaming six-g U-turn. While I don't think the gist of the review is invalidated, it'll probably not reflect the views of a new player. I leave it as an important historical document.[/b]  Overall the game is good, fun and accessible. Supergiant can still deal out a mean action game, and it's still beyond its peers regarding art and sound direction. [i]ok time to nit piiiiiick[/i]  So, mechanics-wise: more moves than original Hades, to the point it gets a little complicated to use your whole arsenal effectively and you'll likely favor two or three moves on each play -- and that's probably how it was intended. The boons and other gifts are a bit over-balanced: a lot of boons amount to the same flat damage bonus to a different move or set of moves, maybe with a little condiment on top.  Funny that it does a Silksong and innovates the gameplay loop by adding a mechanic that's over a decade old and maybe two decades old by this point (quests in silksong and crafting recipes here)  Story-wise: Hades 2 tries to be the inverse of Hades 1. Instead of a cynical layabout, the protagonist is a naïve child soldier. The "home base" is not a house, but a refugee camp. The problem is situational, instead of structural, which makes Melinoe an agent of the status quo instead of a revolutionary. And while Hades was a tormented figure who hid his issues with a broken system behind a duty to the same broken system, Chronos is a scenery-chewing deposed king, whose internal conflict amounts to whether to kill the gods or enslave humanity first.  So this is the anti-Hades I. But the story of Hades I was not just a story of gods; it was carefully tailored to the roguelike genre. You have permadeath, you have a story that carries across loops, you need a way to make the gameplay loop continue after the cutscene, and it all needs to be within budget. That means you can't ever shake the story up enough that gameplay would be altered.  This works in Hades I, whose moral is more or less "a system that incorporates rebellion can remain functional and even improve itself". This does [i]not[/i] work in Hades II. There is no way to end the story and keep it aligned to the roguelike loop without descending into farce. And that's exactly what Hades II does.  Hades 1 was a demonstration of how far you could push storytelling in a roguelike: Hades 2 may be a demonstration of its limits.

text: The ending of this game completely ruined my entire experience. There are several end game momments that just feel like it's making fun of the player for being interested or invested in the narrative, like it was silly of me to care, the conclusion of the hypnos arc is a great example and really felt like a slap in the face.   If you are interested in story do not play this, it will feel like a huge waste of time. HADES 1 is a much better experience in every regard and HADES 2 throws a wet blanket on the entire world narrative. If I could erase this game from my memory I would.

text: This sequel is making me feel like the first one was lightning in a bottle. It's not a bad game. But it just isn't as good as the first Hades.   The environments are all dark and rather boring compared to the bright reds, oranges, and greens that were everywhere in the first one.   The characters don't have much personality and their dialogue is far shorter and less compelling.   Whereas Hades 1 drew me into the world instantly and surrounded me with compelling characters to interact with... this one is making me feel like I'm already supposed to be invested in the story and characters, despite doing nothing for it to happen. The dynamic between Zagreus and Hades was just much more interesting than Melinoë and Hecate's dynamic.  The combat feels less satisfying. The amount of rooms I was in where I was able to just stand still and spam my attacks to get through it were surprisingly high in number. Considering a fair amount of boons involve you standing still to get magic back make me think it's not even a mistake that it's happening. Many of the enemies just don't have movements or attacks that create interesting fights. Some enemies also seem unusually tanky so the fight just feels like a drag because you're dodging the same simple attacks over and over again while slowly chipping away at an HP bar.   I'm not a fan of the progress systems, either. The mirror in the first one and how you upgraded your home just felt more straightforward and rewarding than the cauldron and tarot cards. The way it wants you to collect multiple different resources in order to get upgrades just feel unnecessarily grind-y.  All-in-all it feels like a lot of the stuff in Hades 2 is simply there because it was in Hades 1. But the heart and reason for why those things are there is missing. Right now I'd give this a 6/10. It'd probably be higher if Hades 1 didn't already exist, though. It's just not easy to live up to something that basically attained perfection.  I'm thinking I'm going to refund this for now and wait until 1.0 comes out to try again. Maybe things will be better then and I won't feel like I'm playing an inferior version of Hades. Until then this did make me want to go back and play Hades 1 more so I'll be there for now.

text: I really want to like this game, I really do, but right now, I can only leave a negative review. First Hades was objectively better than Hades II and it makes me sad.  Firstly, the enemies, especially the elites and bosses feel like damage sponges. I never felt this way in the first game, even when I had no idea how to make OP builds to clear the run in like 10 minutes or so. Weapons feel weird and weak, the fights feel sluggish and tedious because of the removal of two dashes, the sprint mechanic just doesn't do it for me. In the first game fights felt quick and snappy, weapons were amazing, easy to understand and use, boons felt more impactful too, here they feel similar to each other and not very impactful, a lot of them are objectively weak.  Secondly, roadblocks are absolutely terrible in this game. I get it, they put Eris to stop the player from progressing too fast and skipping major events and dialogues, but the fact that Eris appears so many times and basically goes "Nuh uh, you don't get to finish the next area" is extremely annoying. In the first game you could finish the game during your first run and even get some extra dialogue, but here you are forced to simply die mid run "because we need you to die right here, sorry mate". And that's only one roadblock that fortunately goes away after a few times. Which brings us to the third point.  Metaprogression. Oh boy... I can't really say anything positive about this. The game feels a lot (and I mean A LOT) more grindy than the first one. There is so many resources you need to keep track off and gather in so many different areas. Some you can only buy at the shop, some you need to grow in your garden and they won't grow unless you go for another run. The fact that they limited the player to just ONE specific tool and thought it's a good idea to stretch the gameplay this way says a lot. Thankfully they fixed it and now you carry all of your tools, but that doesn't fix the issue of having to grind so many resources to buy some unnecessary things at the hub that should be free from the start or even progress the story. Remember Eris? Well, now you've opened the overworld, you think you can just go and experience a new area? Nope, you only have like 1.5 minutes before you die because we need you to stop progressing so quickly! Go and gather some resources to cast a thing that makes you able to stay on the surface without dying in like a minute. And oh, by the way, those resources are in the same area you have a minute to explore. Good luck!  Thanatos encounters were also a lot better than Nemesis ones simply because it was designed in a better way. You had a window to finish the foes he marked or lure them out of his AOE, but here Nemesis just oneshots everything and then leaves while taking one of your options for the next room. Oh, you wanted to get a hammer? Tough luck! Go get those coins for the shop you don't need, sucker!  Chronos and Hades. Oh man... The villain in this game simply sucks. While Hades felt like a very complex character with his set of inner conflicts and such, Chronos is your generic "I'm better than you, I'm time itself, I'm a real baddie here, you all go to a time prison cuz I'm baaad". Same thing goes for the main character. "Chronos bad, kill Chronos, Chronos Chronos Chronos". She goes nowhere near being as charismatic as Zagreus was. And don't even get me started about the Chronos fight. One shots, unpausing your game until you buy another damn upgrade to stop him from doing that (I get it, it's kind of cool that he is a titan of time and all, but you can't tell me this isn't a terrible mechanic), basically no telegraphing for some of his attacks... Fight with Hades was relatively simple, but still tough and he didn't need those oneshot mechanics and no telegraphing animations for his attacks to beat your butt.  I could go for a long time, cuz I do have more issues with this game, like character design, enemy design and a lot more, but this review already looks like an essay. Unfortunately there is pretty much no chance they are going to fix some major issues this game has. I honestly believe we shouldn't tell the developers that these mechanics are okay and praise them for it, but 94% positive reviews are going to tell them a different story. Which is sad. I'm probably going to finish this game once it comes out of Early Access, but that doesn't mean I'm going to like these new mechanics they put in the game to artifically increase the amount of time you have to spend grinding instead of enjoying the game in order to make progress and their balance decisions. It's a real shame that Hades is a lot better than Hades II, I've been waiting for this game and was really hyped, but the experience I got was simply disappointing.

text: I will check back in a few months with the next big update but my hopes aren't high.  If you expect the action of Hades 1 but bigger and better, you will be dissappointed. The introduction of a spell system (omega system) with mana ressources and hold-to-execute attacks is antithetical to the fast and frantic fighting of Hades 1 and a really bad fit to all the features and paradigms they kept.  Unfortunately the mana based actions are now a central component, and in their effort to make you engage with that system, they severely debuffed the effectiveness and fun factor of using "normal" attacks and specials, which was the main driving force of fighting in Hades 1. Also they replaced dashing with a sprint (which is basically like riding a unicycle). There is only single dash no more swift chain dashing... and no, there are no boons for that.  Overall they basically changed the character class of the hero of the game and with all their characterbuilding options still do not allow you reconstruct the "fighter" archetype of Hades 1. But they also did not figure out how to build a game around that new "spell caster "achetype, so a lot of stumpy remains of the features from Hades 1 remain without having much meaning.  In addition they replaced the straightfoward ressource spending of Hades 1 with a crafting system, where you you buy random objects with random recipes, completely torpedoing the goal and strategy driven upgrades system of the first game.  Just meaningless feature creep all around, no innovation. Just unwieldy mechanics and systems and then on top of that more mechancis and systems to make the unwieldy stuff bearable and force you to engage.  You get more Hades content  a lot more - and that is great. But don't expect more Hades gameplay...not to mention an evolution of it. The curiosity for new content currently drives me playing it, but the combat and upgrade gameplay has me disengage more and more with each run.

text: This game is just a better version of Hades. Although the main character is not as charming as Zagreus ( Protagonist of Hades ) and overall the cast of characters seem to be less fun to interact with overall (so far, although this might change with the full release), the gameplay and the soundtrack just blows the first game out of the water. Each weapon is really unique and something you will only find in this game.   Overall, Hades 2 is just a more polished version of Hades. The less charming cast, although charming still,  as compared to Hades 1 is an extremely minor critique of the game and based on my own opinion.  The gameplay is extremely fun, the music is great and the bosses are fantastic (yes, every single one of them). The game also looks extremely pretty and visuals are very charming.   This game goes down as one of the best (if not the best) single player games I have every played. If you like Hades 1, this is a must. If you haven't played Hades 1, then buy Hades 1 first. text: i think I can safely say that Hades II is already a worthwhile succesor to my favourite action yapping-like.   Currently there are 6/7 stages, 6.5 bosses (one is infrequent), 5/6 weapons with 3 aspects each, 2/3 animal familiars, 4 gathering tools, 25 arcana cards, 10 boon gods (12 including sporadic artemis and chaos, 13 if you count spoiler npc god), 15 new chaos trials and 27 keepsakes.  New gods: Hera, Hestia, Apollo, Hephaestus and Selene. Hephaestus is amazing, easily one of the best gods overall. Hera's Hitch mechanic is alright. But Apollo and Hestia are kind of mid right now. Apollo's Daze is weak and I think Hestia's Scorch just does not work properly. Selene introduces new mechanic of ultimate attack based on the mana used during a run. Once you take one ultimate, next boons will provide you with upgrades to it. Pretty fun but once I started focusing more on basic attacks builds and priming mana for benefits, it was completely useless.  Rest of the gods: Zeus and Poseidon are power houses. Aphrodite is killing in close comabt builds while Demeter's frost mechanic plays just great. Meanwhile, Hermes feels like a copy paste from Hades I. Chaos and Artemis are alright but negligable. Spoiler npc god can nerf last boss quite significantly so I always take him.  Gameplay wise it's quite different experience from Hades I. Here it's best if you decide early whether you are going for omega/mana or basic attacks build because focusing too much on both can hurt in the long run. Arcana cards are quite helpful with that but sometimes boons roll for other build than you have arcana cards equipped and it can be not that fun.  Soundtrack 10/10. Whoever designed Oceanus vibes and music, hats off you.  New systems: Arcana cards are new passives but there is a limit to how much you can take at once. Limit can be enhanced but even at max it was still a limit in my experience. Pets are fun, chaos trials are alright, gatherig tools are a little annoying that you can take only one a run but pets offset that a little bit. New interaction mechanics are fun but it seems they are one time only. Why?   Lastly, pet system is weirdly unlocked and can be blocked behind never ending Hecate's yapping if you progress too far too fast. It was literally one of the last things I unlocked after beating last bosses more than 10 times because Hecate was focusing more on what I wore that run rather than giving me animal familiar spell.

text: Hades 1, once i eventually bought it quickly became one of my favorite games to play. I liked the way the story was presented, how you get bits an pieces.   Hades 2 as i consider it, is a sequel as a sequel should be. Some mechanics stayed the same, though some changes may require you to relearn that muscle memory a bit, which i think is a plus.  Like Hades 1, i love the aesthetic once again, the voice acting. Even though the game is not complete (yet), it doesn't feel you are playing a demo. Hell, i feel like i'm getting so much more from this early access than a lot of AAA 'completed' titles recently.  Supergiant Games once again has made promises that have been delivered.   The wait was worth the time, but now's the time that time must die.   DEATH TO KRONOS.

text: There's a lot of people complaining in the reviews about the new combat mechanics. I agree that there is much changed from the first game, but I think that's a good thing. If I wanted to play more Hades I, I would play Hades I.  In my experience, any time I thought a weapon or other mechanism (like the sprint, hex, and omega moves) were weird or too weak, I found some way to use them that actually gave me a massive boost. I ended up beating the underworld and surface for the first time with weapons I thought were odd. I've found that Hades II requires more strategizing and thoughtfulness than Hades I, which made the game more rewarding for me.  It is also still early access; the story is incomplete, so wait until full release if you want a complete story and closure.

text: A wonderful game that's been refined and polished to an extreme degree during the early access phase - the amount of care and love SPG has put into this is obvious from the get-go, from the overall narrative to the smallest details. A lot of the DNA from Hades 1 is here (adjustable difficulty, interesting retellings of Greek mythology, gorgeous artwork and music...) but Hades 2 puts its own spin on the formula with combat I found easier to pick up than Hades 1 (as a casual player), a slightly different tone and a bigger scope. I'm just happy to see a great game like this do this well and I can't wait to keep playing.

text: After 100 hours in, I can honestly say that Hades II is not only a great successor to one of the best roguelikes ever made - it’s actually even better.  The number of possible builds and weapons that completely change the way you play is outstanding (I’ve already lost count of how many new “favorite” builds I’ve had…). And the best part is that you’re constantly discovering something new! The pace at which new mechanics and content are introduced is extremely well designed - really, folks from Supergiant mastered this art in their games. Lastly, just like in Hades, the sheer amount of content is impressive. I’m more than 100 runs in and still unlocking new dialogue lines or prophecies.  If you’re new to the series, Hades might be more beginner-friendly, but you can absolutely start here without missing out. It’s pure fun!  Side note: Steam Deck performance is top-notch. No tweaking needed.

text: The true ending of Hades II on 1.0 release felt unsatisfying and rushed, especially when comparing it to Hades and Pyre. I enjoyed the outcome of it, but it lacked good execution and did not have nearly enough "show, don't tell" for a game that was in development for four and a half years. That being said, I still considered every other aspect of the game to be outstanding.   I gotta give major props to Supergiant for changing the true ending, as well as its build-up & aftermath in the upcoming Patch 1. The altered post-victory dialogue with [spoiler]Zagreus[/spoiler] and new true ending scenes have addressed every single problem I had with the writing. It still perplexes me why SG didn't just release 1.0 later, but I couldn't be happier with how they addressed the criticism. 10/10 game with what is probably my favorite soundtrack of all time.

text: After 200+ hours, Hades II still surprises me. Actually… it’s closer to 340 hours now, and that’s not even counting the time I spent on the early access build. No regrets.  The game is full of brilliant little design choices. One moment that hit me early on was during the Chronos fight. When I desperately paused to go pee, and he just screamed “Time cannot be STOPPED!” I swear I almost peed myself on the spot. And Scylla losing her mind if you mute the music? Perfect.  Even after dozens of runs, I kept finding new dialogue, new reactions, and even a completely new Scylla song I never expected to hear that late in the game.  Every character feels unique and oddly respectable. Even the “gross” ones like Eris, Narcissus, or Scylla. Not every weapon aspect feels dramatically different (I genuinely can’t feel much difference between Zorephet Melinoë and Charon aspects), but the mix of boons, weapon choices, and keepsakes keeps runs feeling fresh. The way the game encourages swapping keepsakes between regions is great. It keeps the flow dynamic.  My biggest frustration is with some prophets that depend entirely on RNG, like collecting every legendary or duo boon. Those don’t test skill. just perseverance and patience.  But everything else? Absolutely stunning. The world, the art, the soundtrack, the atmosphere. Crossroads, Olympus, and especially Scylla & The Sirens (with Charybdis!) are breathtaking. It’s a beautiful, surprising, endlessly enjoyable sequel.  P.S. I liked the early-access fishing more.

text: [h1] Hades II is A Perfect Sequel [/h1]  Razor-sharp art direction, buttery smooth animations, instantly readable visual language, it's all here. All refined and polished to an exceptional quality. Every environment feels dense with personality. Every character is designed with unique flair. Every animation feels handcrafted with love, care, and obsession. This game’s art direction oozes confidence. The subtle and quiet kind of confidence that comes from a studio who knows exactly who they are, and what they’re good at.  And if there’s anything Supergiant Games are good at, it’s combat. Fast, fluid, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Attacks snap with weight. Dashes feel precise. Abilities are unique and flashy. You are constantly in motion, constantly adapting, constantly making micro-decisions, and it results in a cripplingly addictive gameplay loop that will constantly have you itching for more and more runs.  The new mechanics and weapons layer beautifully onto that foundation. They create a stronger emphasis on spacing, timing, and positioning. The introduction of magick adds onto that complexity a new layer of balance and build variety. It expands the player expression in meaningful ways, and when your build comes together, the game reaches satisfying dopamine heights you will never forget.  And just as unforgettable is the game’s story. A melancholic tale wrapped in mythology, family, destiny, and defiance. The writing is sharp, intimate, and surprisingly intelligent. Characters feel real, with each one bringing unique personality and emotion. The dialogue is natural, sometimes witty, but emotionally grounded. And with each completed run, you unlock new dialogues, new faces, new interactions. Every return to the main hub soon begins to feel like coming home. You begin to feel a sense of familiarity.  [h3] And that’s Hades II's biggest failure. Familiarity. [/h3]  No matter how polished, how expanded, how refined the systems are, the core loop feels deeply recognizable. If you’ve poured dozens (or hundreds) of hours into the first Hades like I have, you will immediately understand Hades II.   That’s both its greatest strength and its quietest weakness. Because while everything here is better, smoother, and more ambitious, very little of it feels revolutionary. The structure, pacing, and rhythm of progression are largely unchanged. You’re chasing upgrades, unlocking weapons, deepening relationships, repeating runs, and slowly unraveling the story.  It’s excellent. It works. But it’s also incredibly safe.  At a certain point, that sense of discovery that defined the original begins to dull. Not because the game becomes bad, but because your brain already knows the language it’s speaking. You’ve spent countless hours studying it already. You’re already fluent in it. It makes the mystery thinner, the surprises smaller, the experience more predictable. The magic is still there. It just doesn’t hit quite as hard as the first Hades.   The balance is also lacking. Some builds feel wildly more powerful than others. Experimentation feels more punished than encouraged. Certain runs snowball into effortless dominance, while others feel like uphill slogs dictated more by RNG than skill. The bosses are well-designed and visually striking, and yet still begin to blur together mechanically over long play sessions. You learn their patterns. You solve their puzzles. And very quickly their sense of danger fades, and so does their novelty.  What was once exhilarating becomes procedural. And that’s the heart of Hades II’s biggest problem. It’s so damn good that you expect it to constantly amaze you. But perfection is not sustainable.   [h2] Conclusion [/h2]  This is a phenomenal game. A beautifully crafted, expertly designed, lovingly written action roguelike that delivers moment-to-moment excellence with absurd consistency. It just doesn’t redefine the genre the way its predecessor did. And maybe that’s an unfair expectation. Because what Hades II ultimately is, is a masterclass in iteration. Not a revolution. Not a reinvention. Just a refinement of a formula that already worked. This is comfort food for people who love this style of game. Very high-quality comfort food.  Hades II is excellent. Not flawless. Not groundbreaking. But deeply, undeniably excellent. And sometimes, that’s enough. It's certainly enough for me.  That is why Hades II is the perfect sequel, and that is why I can't recommend it enough.   8.7/10

The subtle and quiet kind of confidence that comes from a studio who knows exactly who they are, and what they’re good at.  And if there’s anything Supergiant Games are good at, it’s combat. Fast, fluid, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Attacks snap with weight. Dashes feel precise. Abilities are unique and flashy. You are constantly in motion, constantly adapting, constantly making micro-decisions, and it results in a cripplingly addictive gameplay loop that will constantly have you itching for more and more runs.  The new mechanics and weapons layer beautifully onto that foundation. They create a stronger emphasis on spacing, timing, and positioning. The introduction of magick adds onto that complexity a new layer of balance and build variety. It expands the player expression in meaningful ways, and when your build comes together, the game reaches satisfying dopamine heights you will never forget.  And just as unforgettable is the game’s story. A melancholic tale wrapped in mythology, family, destiny, and defiance. The writing is sharp, intimate, and surprisingly intelligent. Characters feel real, with each one bringing unique personality and emotion. The dialogue is natural, sometimes witty, but emotionally grounded. And with each completed run, you unlock new dialogues, new faces, new interactions. Every return to the main hub soon begins to feel like coming home. You begin to feel a sense of familiarity.  [h3] And that’s Hades II's biggest failure. Familiarity. [/h3]  No matter how polished, how expanded, how refined the systems are, the core loop feels deeply recognizable. If you’ve poured dozens (or hundreds) of hours into the first Hades like I have, you will immediately understand Hades II.   That’s both its greatest strength and its quietest weakness. Because while everything here is better, smoother, and more ambitious, very little of it feels revolutionary. The structure, pacing, and rhythm of progression are largely unchanged. You’re chasing upgrades, unlocking weapons, deepening relationships, repeating runs, and slowly unraveling the story.  It’s excellent. It works. But it’s also incredibly safe.  At a certain point, that sense of discovery that defined the original begins to dull. Not because the game becomes bad, but because your brain already knows the language it’s speaking. You’ve spent countless hours studying it already. You’re already fluent in it. It makes the mystery thinner, the surprises smaller, the experience more predictable. The magic is still there. It just doesn’t hit quite as hard as the first Hades.   The balance is also lacking. Some builds feel wildly more powerful than others. Experimentation feels more punished than encouraged. Certain runs snowball into effortless dominance, while others feel like uphill slogs dictated more by RNG than skill. The bosses are well-designed and visually striking, and yet still begin to blur together mechanically over long play sessions. You learn their patterns. You solve their puzzles. And very quickly their sense of danger fades, and so does their novelty.  What was once exhilarating becomes procedural. And that’s the heart of Hades II’s biggest problem. It’s so damn good that you expect it to constantly amaze you. But perfection is not sustainable.   [h2] Conclusion [/h2]  This is a phenomenal game. A beautifully crafted, expertly designed, lovingly written action roguelike that delivers moment-to-moment excellence with absurd consistency. It just doesn’t redefine the genre the way its predecessor did. And maybe that’s an unfair expectation. Because what Hades II ultimately is, is a masterclass in iteration. Not a revolution. Not a reinvention. Just a refinement of a formula that already worked. This is comfort food for people who love this style of game. Very high-quality comfort food.  Hades II is excellent. Not flawless. Not groundbreaking. But deeply, undeniably excellent. And sometimes, that’s enough. It's certainly enough for me.  That is why Hades II is the perfect sequel, and that is why I can't recommend it enough.   8.7/10

text: Hades II is a remarkably confident action roguelike that expands the foundations of its predecessor without simply repeating them. Developed and published by Supergiant Games, the game shifts attention to Melinoë, Princess of the Underworld and a witch trained for an immense task: defeating Chronos, the Titan of Time. This change in protagonist gives the sequel its own identity, with witchcraft, ritual magic, and a broader interpretation of Greek mythology shaping both its story and gameplay. The result feels familiar enough for returning players while introducing enough new ideas to stand comfortably on its own.  Combat remains the central attraction, but Melinoë approaches battles differently. Her Weapons of Night provide distinct fighting styles, and each weapon can be transformed through combinations of attacks, specials, casts, Omega techniques, and divine Boons. Omega abilities are particularly important because they consume Magick and encourage more deliberate decisions about positioning and resource management. Instead of constantly attacking without thought, players are rewarded for understanding when to charge a powerful technique, when to reposition, and when to preserve Magick for a more dangerous encounter.  The Boon system continues to make individual runs unpredictable and highly replayable. Olympian gods can modify attacks and abilities in ways that encourage experimentation, allowing a weapon to perform dramatically differently from one attempt to another. Some combinations emphasize raw damage, while others reward mobility, status effects, defensive play, ranged pressure, or carefully timed abilities. Not every combination becomes equally powerful, and disappointing builds are possible, but discovering unexpected synergies is a major part of the appeal. The large number of variables ensures that mastering the game involves understanding systems rather than memorizing one perfect strategy.  Progression between runs is considerably more involved than simply improving combat statistics. The Altar of Ashes provides permanent customization, while reagents gathered during expeditions contribute to various forms of advancement. Tools of the Unseen make resource collection an active part of exploration, and witchy familiars add another useful and charming element to Melinoë's growing collection of abilities. These mechanics strengthen the feeling that every expedition accomplishes something. Even a failed run can produce materials, knowledge, relationship development, or upgrades that influence what happens next.  The world itself is one of the sequel's greatest achievements. Environments have striking hand-painted presentation and clearly differentiated atmospheres, while enemies and hazards force players to adjust their tactics as they advance. The expanded journey beyond the Underworld also gives the conflict greater scale. Chronos feels like a threat affecting an entire mythological order, and the environments reinforce the impression that Melinoë is participating in a prolonged campaign rather than simply attempting a sequence of dungeon escapes.  Storytelling remains closely integrated with repetition. Returning after defeat rarely feels like merely restarting because characters frequently have something new to say. Gods, witches, shades, monsters, and other mythological figures react to Melinoë's progress and previous encounters. Conversations gradually reveal relationships, personal histories, rivalries, and details about the larger struggle. Melinoë is also sufficiently different from Zagreus in personality and motivation. She carries herself with greater discipline and purpose, which suits a protagonist raised and trained specifically for her mission.  Presentation is consistently excellent. Detailed environments, expressive character artwork, smooth real-time animation, magical visual effects, and an energetic soundtrack give the game a strong personality. Battles can become extremely busy when numerous enemies, projectiles, and magical effects fill the screen, but visual feedback is generally clear enough to keep the action readable. Voice acting is another major strength, helping even short conversations feel worthwhile and giving the large cast distinctive personalities.  Difficulty is challenging but flexible. Players who enjoy mastering enemy patterns and increasingly demanding encounters have plenty of opportunities to test themselves, while God Mode offers an alternative for those who primarily want to experience the narrative and progression without becoming trapped by the difficulty curve. Permanent upgrades also mean that persistence gradually improves the player's options. This creates an effective balance between mechanical skill and long-term progression without making victory feel automatic.  The game does have potential drawbacks. Its fundamental structure requires repeated runs through familiar locations, so anyone who dislikes roguelikes may still find the repetition exhausting. Resource gathering adds meaningful progression but can occasionally make an expedition feel driven by collecting materials rather than pursuing the strongest possible combat route. The abundance of currencies, upgrades, Boons, weapons, and interconnected systems can also feel overwhelming during the opening hours. Some randomly assembled builds are noticeably less effective than others, making occasional runs feel disadvantaged by poor synergy.  Steam Deck compatibility is excellent. Hades II is Steam Deck Verified, meaning its primary functionality works with the handheld's controls and display, its interface text is considered readable, and its default graphics configuration is suitable for the device. The relatively compact encounter-based structure is particularly well suited to portable play, allowing a player to complete a few chambers or undertake a longer run depending on available time.  Ultimately, Hades II succeeds because it treats a sequel as an opportunity to deepen and reinterpret a proven formula. Its combat is responsive, its build possibilities are extensive, and its permanent progression provides constant motivation to attempt another run. More importantly, gameplay progression and storytelling support each other exceptionally well. Failure advances relationships and knowledge while success opens additional challenges and possibilities. Supergiant Games has produced a sequel with enough mechanical and narrative personality to avoid living entirely in the shadow of the original.  For players who appreciate action roguelikes, Greek mythology, build experimentation, challenging combat, and character-driven storytelling, Hades II is an exceptional package. A few systems can become complicated and repetition remains unavoidable, but those weaknesses are outweighed by the tremendous combat variety, polished presentation, compelling characters, rewarding progression, and sheer density of meaningful content. It is the kind of game where finishing a run often produces the immediate temptation to start another.  Rating: 10/10

text: Hades 2 is a textbook case of a game sequel becoming lesser because it added more to it.   On its surface, Putting More Greek Myth Into Hades is fine. Having two different runs you can do? Cool. It's more content to explore. Past that novelty though it starts to feel overstuffed when you realize what that means - it's also (many) more material grinds. It's more feature and quality of life unlocks you need to perform. It's more content that you might need to interact with for progression that can work at cross purposes to itself - maybe you need bronze and wool to make a new tool but the weapon with a bonus that run has a testament to kill a boss in the Underworld. Maybe a prophecy requires you to go to the surface but you need to track down a NPC in the Underworld. Pick what you actually care about. It's not total isolation of the content across the two runs, but it makes it feel a lot of the time like you're getting less out of a run than you did in the first game. It's less focused to its detriment. It's not inherently bad that the surface is a lot harder than the Underworld but having to bounce back and forth leads to these weird difficulty peaks and valleys instead of it feeling like smooth progression. Some of the difficulty spikes also feel unrewarding - in Hades 1 I ran Extreme Measures 3 permanently when I unlocked it. I stopped attempting Vow of Rivals fights in H2 because it changes the fights to add a lot more projectile barrages and status effects and make them more punitive to mistakes, not actually more tactically or strategically interesting to engage with.  I think Melinoë has some cool options in terms of combat and builds. The addition of casts as a big AOE field and the Omega skills for each weapon doing different things does lend itself to some fun builds, especially when you start to figure out how you like to use each aspect, or how to pivot during a run to lean into one of them. Hexes are also interesting as a replacement for the summons in the first game. I did struggle in that I had a hard time finding weapons and aspects I legitimately enjoyed using versus just tolerated when I needed to do a particular prophecy or testament.  Overall there's still a fluidity and speed to combat in Hades 2 that matches the first game and it's probably the biggest thing it does have going for it.  I also think Hades 2's story also doesn't really work even independent of the tweaks Supergiant are going to patch in. I didn't hate it, but it suffers from the same sort of Let's Do More And Go Bigger problem that the Hades 2 experience as a whole does. Hades 1 worked in large part because it wasn't a big world-encompassing conflict, it was just the Greek gods being petty and dysfunctional with each other but keeping it in the family, and Zagreus being a voice of reason asking things like "Why the fuck are we preventing Orpheus and Eurydice from being together?" Suddenly in Hades 2 you've got this Titans vs Gods conflict with huge sieges vs Mount Olympus and the Underworld has fallen and the Fates are missing and the gods are arguing about how severely to punish mortals for not keeping up their offerings during all this and it's just really kind of impossible to care about. That's not even getting into the landmines that crop up when making Time itself a story component. The characters were otherwise generally written in that sort of inoffensive young adult story way that you can't really get all that upset over, but there was also a degree of "We used up a bunch of characters in the first game, who's left for us to drag into this" to the proceedings. Being amused at Narcissus sounding like Nicolas Cage only goes so far.  I don't write any of this to say that Hades 2 is a bad game. I wouldn't have put ~75 hours into it in a month if it was. It just felt like that Hollywood style Go Bigger With The Sequel thing hit really hard here. Hades 1 was my easy GOTY in 2020.  Hades 2 is not comparable, and that's ultimately disappointing.

text: Hades 2 gave my Steam Deck controller stick drift, that's how you know it’s a good game. ;( yeap “I’ll be up soon honey - just entertain yourself with your boyfriend and let me do one more run that’s all, I promise.” This game is Crack/Cocaine. It’s like Hades 1, but better. Jokes aside, Hades 2 is the only game I played that was so good in early access, I forced myself to stop playing. It took basically everything that made Hades good and made it better then added extra stuff for fun, as sequels go this is absolutely peak. There’s a reason this is the studio's first sequel. The original Hades was iconic and beloved, and the sequel still has that signature charm while just adding so much more. Every part of this game justifies its existence and every part of it is perfectly balanced and detailed, all while creating an entirely unique personality that separates it from the first. It’s an action pack, fast paced roguelite which also allows you to either have a semi-manual build or a randomized build throughout the run. It's so addicting and each run still brings something new, Supergiant really hit it out of the park. I love the way it fits in with my life, because I can just pick it up for a half-hour run a couple of times during a day and feel totally satisfied with that whereas a couple of half-hour sessions with most AAA action-adventures wouldn't feel satisfying at all. Gameplay is SO GOOD, so many options and variations on how to play and become strong it feels REALLY REALLY GOOD. Animal companions are nice little additions and all the weapons feel like they have a place and builds that make them feel positively busted. While I think some of the story beats have been a bit of a letdown in some degree the characters, writing, worldbuilding all feel positively great. Art is beautiful, character designs are at their peak once again (even better than the OG), gameplay is smooth as butter, and voice acting and music are phenomenal. Seriously as someone who loves some voicework, VA work here is ASTOUNDING. The cast does such a good job, Hecate especially just embodies the character. Old cast is also still great and it was a blast from start to finish. I'm probably gonna hit 100+ hours by the time I finish and that's fine, Supergiant killed it again even with the few gripes I have this game is still worth your time and money. If you're starting from Hades 1 you should keep in mind that you are coming from a game where you built up to being incredibly powerful to, functionally, starting all over here. Go try and play Hades 1 again with a fresh save and see if it feels like the same kind of obstacle. Hades 2 is, admittedly, a bit harder than I found Hades 1. Most significantly the dash, but learning how to use the Sprint is key, here. The starting weapon, is definitely meant to try to train you into using Omega attacks early on to get a feel for how to weave them into your combat and utilize them later in the game. Admittedly, I abused the hell out of the stun-lock by spamming the hell out of Special and staying as far away from whatever was trapped in my Cast as I could. But I genuinely think most people’s biggest obstacle with the combat (especially based on complaints from other reviewers like "enemies having too much health" or "I feel I do no damage") is because of the comparative factor of how far they’ve gotten in Hades 1. Take your time, be patient, and remember that these games are all about that gradual growth. Dying, while frustrating, is always the best teacher. Eventually, once you've got certain things unlocked, you'll start to feel that powerful feeling again and it'll all make sense. Honestly I had a blast with H2. I would not say it's overall better than H1, but there is more of it for sure. I miss some things about H1, and there are some things about H2 that  are better. Overall I'm very satisfied, it is a great iteration on Hades 1 and does a ton of QoL to smooth the experience. If you enjoyed the gameplay loop of the 1st then this is a pretty easy recommendation. Go buy this freaking game, you won’t regret it. 9/10

text: Hades 2 does many things better, and many things worse. My views after having completed the original with 100% achievements.  This game is a lot richer than its predecessor and has many more fun mechanics and items to play around with. I also appreciate that there are two different paths, as it breaks the monotony and can be refreshing. The same goes for the open-field area in the underground.  However, the top side is unfortunately very bad, in my opinion, for multiple reasons. Specifically, the Mount and Summit. The first two regions are great, especially the first one. Once you start the mountain climb, though, it falls apart. Yes, the difficulty is ridiculously dialed up, but that is not my main issue.  My main issue is the boss and level design.  Since it is essentially two regions in one, it becomes very monotonous, and that is made considerably worse by the fact that almost every encounter has the same enemies and takes place in the same kind of boxed-in room. It is tight and creates an absolute mess of visual clutter and enemy numbers without giving you much freedom of movement, which seriously hampers any kind of strategy beyond spraying and praying for the most part.  The bosses are also very lame.  Prometheus will literally stop the fight to play a memory game with you, which is both concentration and immersion-breaking, while also being far too punishing if you miss one, or god forbid, multiple sequences. It can burn through a bunch of your revives. That sequence should automatically end if you trigger a Death Defiance.  The Summit throws multiple hard-hitting bosses at you without giving you any real chance to recuperate or heal before going into the final boss. And that final boss is atrocious.  The fight itself is long and boring. It is essentially a damage sponge where you find yourself running up, throwing a cast and getting a few hits in, then running around, and repeating that ad infinitum. It is so lame that after beating him the first few times, I was reluctant and dreading having to redo that fight. It is simply not fun.  There is challenging difficulty, and then there is cheap difficulty. In a lot of cases, the Summit falls into the latter. That is especially disappointing because the vast majority of the rest of the game is fantastic.  There is so much I want to love about this sequel, but that Mount + Summit section really puts a sour taste in my mouth.  Unrelated side note: I kind of wish all the small talk you have with the gods and companions would actually result in something definitive. It can be fun from a lore perspective, but at the end of the day, you know nothing will come out of all the talking. It is just talk for the sake of talking.  It is interesting at first, but gets annoying as you go on. This was somewhat of a pet peeve of mine since the first game, to be fair. I end up skipping most of it after a couple dozen hours. They speak of solutions and make promises, but you know it will lead to nothing because it cannot. There is no closure, and therefore it gradually loses its value.  If they ever make a third one, I really hope those conversations occasionally lead to something concrete and actionable.

text: It's Hades II in every meaning of the word. If you liked the first one, you will like this, if you didn't, you probably won't. Same gameloop, same playstyle, same writing. There are a bunch of new things the devs are trying out, new types of enemies, new types of locations, new side mechanics. There is now resource farming here, which is integrated pretty well into the gameloop, and surprisingly isn't boring. Also there are now two separate [spoiler]"campaigns", the underworld and the surface, each with its own unique locations and bosses[/spoiler]. So it's not "just another Hades" in a sense that it has nothing new, it definitely does. It changes the formula of the previous game, expands upon it, and doesn't prey upon nostalgia as I honestly feared it would. New things can be hits or misses though. Due to it being Early Access a lot of stuff is unpolished or unfinished, both in terms of gameplay and narrative, so don't buy it yet if you're looking for a complete experience. Though it's still totally worth your money even now.  Good game with the chance of becoming truly exceptional when it finally launches, Death to Chronos/10

text: It's hard for me to properly articulate my disappointment with this game, but I'll try.  First off, this is not a bad game, which is why I still recommend it. But the biggest problem with this game is that it adopted the "bigger is better" method as a sequel, and it's worse off for it. There are more levels to get through, more dialogue among characters, more side content, more abilities, more everything. But it's too much. Things lack focus. The pacing feels bad. The main story is simply not as compelling as the prequel, even though the stakes feel a lot higher.   The core of the issue with the story and characters and the structure of the plot (as it evolves between runs) is that it does not feel novel anymore, because Hades 1 exists. Reimagining Greek myth in this way is no longer as interesting as it once was. I remember encountering the Oceanus boss for the first time and smiling to myself. The rest of the game is not nearly as charming.  But all of that could still be compelling if the writing was actually good. But it's not. It's thoroughly researched and appropriately delivered. But ultimately there's a lot of talking that means very little. To be clear this might have been an issue with Hades 1 as well, but the whole concept was novel enough not to notice. The same grace doesn't extend to Hades II. Melinoe as a stubbornly sincere and straightforward character really starts to wear by the end. She is simply not as fun to follow through a story as Zagreus was, even though the only real difference between the two is that Zagreus had a more obvious sense of humour. I don't want to call it as bad as the slander that newer Insomniac games get, but the fact that I'm even comparing the two should tell you everything.  The true ending has all the impact of a small fart by the time you finally grind enough to get there. When I finally finished the epilogue, I was certain that I'd spent far more time playing Hades II compared to the prequel, and I was genuinely shocked to find out that I was still more than 10 hours behind. I rolled credits on Hades at around 75 hours, and continued to play till I hit over 110 hours on the highest heat I could manage while completing every prophecy on the list. With Hades II, I rolled credits around 90 hours, saw the story related prophecies on the list, and realised that if I didn't do them now, I would never do them. Because I didn't want to play anymore.  The difference is that I couldn't get enough of Hades 1, and I couldn't wait to be done with Hades II.

text: I hate to give this a negative review, but my instant emotional reaction to the ending (yes, the updated one present in the review patch!) is so overwhelmingly poor that I find myself earnestly annoyed at the thought of this narrative continuing into the post-game. Like everyone else says, the gameplay rocks, but jesus christ that ending.  In Hades 1, the in-universe reason Zagreus would continue to try and escape was simple and elegant: it's his job now. There, done. The narrative played out in exactly the way it had to, and the game continuing to be playable didn't hurt it at all—rather, it felt like it becoming his job was more of a happy coincidence than a purposeful, pre-planned idea that *had* to happen.  The opposite is true in Hades 2. The vibe I get is that the writers were *obsessed* with recapturing that simple elegance of the first game's in-universe justification for why the game can keep being played, to the point where it screwed over the narrative conclusion. I can imagine several different ways the game could keep being played, and yet the writers chose the worst one.  The player does not care for Chronos. We are told, repeatedly, over and over, that he is a monster that, unfortunately, must have his immortality stripped away and killed permanently. And, in the 35 runs it took me to complete the game, that belief was never challenged by anyone except Eris, the embodiment of Strife who loves it when things are awful for everyone else, and Chronos himself, the guy who has kidnapped your family.  Yet, right when we're about to finish him off, there is a sudden proposition of, "Guys... what if he's just misunderstood?" As if it doesn't matter that the reason he was chopped up by the gods was that he ate all of his kids. And then it turns out, yes, he is just misunderstood! All he wanted was a family, aww. And of course, the best way to portray this to the player is through an ~2 minute montage where we see an alternate world in which he isn't a mass murderer of mortals and serial kidnapper! A world where, conveniently, we also don't see how Hades and everyone else forgives him for the crime of eating babies!  And then because there's a *chance* he was a good person in a different timeline and he feels bad for it, we should spare him. Power of family for the win! After that, he becomes our kooky, silly grandpa. How heart-warming!  The plot-twist of Death to Chronos being, "Death to the evil personality of Chronos" is so utterly jarring that I did not care to even pay attention during the credits, a remarkable feat considering Hades 1's "In the Blood" boat-ride through all the layers of the Underworld is up there as one of my favorite moments in gaming. Instead, I was looking online to confirm that, yes, most other people also despise this ending.  Part of what I loved about Chronos was how much of a bastard he was. After giving Mel a brief chance, he promptly switches to being the Worst Guy Ever, and that rules. He was mean, demeaning, sneering, believing himself above literally everything. That's gone when you roll credits. He simply becomes good after getting memories transplanted into him.   Imagine if that happened in Hades 1. Imagine if, instead of a very gradual change developed through dozens and dozens of runs, Hades behaved the exact same as he does when he berates Zagreus at the beginning until the moment Persephone came back to the Underworld, and suddenly he becomes a loving father without any of his past flaws! That is what they did with Chronos, except instead of an immortal, overworked, overprotective dad who acted in a flawed but understandable way, Chronos wants to kill the gods or something (they never make it quite clear what he wants, considering he didn't kill the Cthonic gods).  I can see a world where this idea of redeeming Chronos works. However, that world require altering the majority of dialogues with Chronos, tons of dialogue with other characters, and greatly expanding the post-narrative to include even *more* development for Chronos. Because as it is, the writers have thrown their hands up at actually writing *how* Chronos becomes better. Isn't it awesome how those transplanted memories solve the issue of actually getting people to like Chronos? And how his judgement in Olympus is entirely passed over as well? We don't need to show that to the audience, they already know that he was a good guy in an alternate timeline, that's good enough!  Instead of having to change all this dialogue and stuff to make the ending *salvagable*, they could've just taken the story in a different direction. Maybe follow through with "Death to Chronos"?  Although this review is largely about the ending, the post-game narrative is also really bizarre. I've only done a few runs (again, not much motivation to do so), and a lot of dialogue is... weird. Different characters keep saying the same phrases, "so that time can flow freely" and "the possibility of", which not only sounds really bad when every character says the exact same thing to refer to it, but it's also nonsensical. What does the possibility of Typhon or Chronos returning mean? Who knows! The game hasn't told me. I mentioned at the beginning that it seems the writers here were too wrapped up in creating a good in-universe reason for the game to continue, but they failed even at that while still sacrificing the climax of the story. (Also, really cool that we just don't get to see the House of Hades or Olympus anymore! That's so awesome! I don't care about those places anyway! Who would???????)  That was a very rambling review and contains maybe 1/3 of my thoughts on it. To reiterate, the gameplay is electric, but I cannot recommend this game when the ending and post-game make me so upset and annoyed that I don't really want to play more. If you need me, I'll be on Ao3 reading (or writing, if it doesn't exist) a fanfiction where Mel carries through with her task.

text: Gameplay-wise, it's indubitably a good game. It's slicker and deeper than its predecessor, and has that addicting quality: since you allocate the rewards after the run, you're naturally guided to start the next one to check them out.  But in terms of story, meaning, and substance — it's a complete nothingburger. Hades was a teenage drama, a game about a boy's separation from his domineering father and reconnecting with his absent mother, wrapped in the metaphor of ancient Greek myth. Hades II is just fantasy with no additional layer, a jumble of random connections that somehow shifts the focus from Melinoe to Zagreus and drowns in fan service. The bad guy in the first game was your father, intent on controlling you. The bad guy here is just a fantasy dude.  I had fun with the sessions I played. And then I laid the controller down — and nothing would ever compel me to take it up again, because this game, while very well-executed, is completely devoid of everything that made the first one special. It feel like fan fiction made by a different team that tries to mimic the glamor and misses the point.

text: Yea. It's amazing like the reviews say it is. I don't play a lot of Roguelikes/RogueLites but I was really drawn to this one. I was drawn to this for the very reason that some people might find annoying.   I LOVE, excessive amounts of dialogue.   I LOVE, slamming my head against a wall over and over. This game is a manifestation of several things I love about gaming and about video games in general. If you happen to hate any of these maybe wait to get the game on sale. If you hate all of these. The first game also has everything I mentioned above. this game simply took that formula and made it better and ... yea, that's it. It's fun and you should get it.   Side note, just a small anecdote, there's an explicit mod to make the game goon friendly that's VERY easy to install. which I also recommend.

text: This is one of the greatest Early Access releases of recent times:  • Optimization is on-point (90FPS on Steam Deck with the highest settings and 6 hours battery life? yo?) The soundtrack is something else.  • Combat has improved a LOT: way more diverse with the magic spells, button pressures and power combinations... generally feels way more snappy than the 1st Hades which already had a GREAT combat system.  Can't complain when a sequel is a "more of the same" improving in every aspect of its predecessor in such a magnificent way.  Not a fan of Early Access as selling system but I support the way Hades II has been thrown on the market 'cause it feels way more polished and complete than most games coming out in their 1.0 versions.

text: Hades II improves on the original in many ways. Combat is deeper, builds are more complex, and the overall systems feel more refined and ambitious. There’s clearly more content, more mechanics, and more room to experiment.  That said, it doesn’t quite capture the special feeling of the first game. The pacing is slower, the tone is heavier, and the characters don’t hit as instantly as before. Some new systems feel a bit overdesigned, adding complexity without always increasing fun.  Overall, it’s a strong and impressive sequel — just not as iconic or emotionally sharp as the original.  Recommended, but with tempered expectations.

text: While I can safely recommend this game for anyone to buy, I recommend that with a caveat as my biggest criticism with this game is likely something that will NOT be changed. That problem is visual clarity. In many fights, especially with Vow of Rivals bosses, there is so much visual vomit between boss attacks, Melinoe's attacks, and boon effects that it is practically impossible to properly react to everything on the screen. Many attacks barely register visually, while others overpower almost anything, causing other projectiles and attacks to be practically invisible. These visuals actually kill any desire I have to fight Vow of Rivals boss variants as they just become frustrating bullet hells where I can barely even see the bullets. That being said, I greatly enjoy all other aspects of the game, from the weapons, to the characters, and the locations. As it stands right now, I would give the game an 8.5/10. If it wasn't for the issue of visual clarity I could probably give this game a solid 10/10 but unless the visuals are tweaked that's where my option stands.   TLDR: Buy the game, but definitely expect some frustrations born out of visual clutter rather than genuine difficulty later on.

text: [h1] Should you buy it in Early Access? [/h1]  That's kind of the big question. There's quite a lot of content available in the game right now and I've unlocked everything major. Hades 2 is a ton of fun, but as you might expect from early access the content abruptly ends at some point and you'll have to wait until the next update. While it is fun, there are also some kinks and pacing issues that will be ironed out over EA, so I would recommend waiting if you're not impatient like me.  The big issue with EA is obviously the story. When you beat the final boss, the story abruptly ends and you don't get to know what happens next. There's a couple of unresolved side stories as well,   Gameplay-wise, Hades 2 is awesome. It's as satisfying as you might expect from a sequel to Hades 1. The bosses are also a massive step up in quality, they're a lot more fun and creative.   There's some balance issues but something that really needs tweaking is omega abilities (charging attacks). If you base your build around charging attacks the combat becomes kind of tedious since you slow down time every time you charge, and you're incentivized to use your mana actively but it can feel like it takes forever to use it up.  You won't run into this in most runs, but when you have an omega attack build you'll quickly realize you have to hold attack for one second, release, and repeat 20 times until combat is over. All the while time slows down, which can bring the pacing of the combat down with it and it turns into a bit of a waiting game where you stand still and spam. Supergiant have acknowledged this and I trust they'll figure it out in time.  The one thing I am a bit worried about is the writing. The story is still excellent of course, but like others have mentioned it feels more dry than Hades 1. Melinoe isn't as interesting as Zagreus, her mission comes down to "I want to kill Chronos" and isn't very personal.  Hades 1 had a lot of fun dynamics like Zagreus' spiteful relationship with his father, his awkward friendship with Dusa and Meg, his funny rivalry with Theseus, etc. This game is lacking a bit of that energy. A lot of dialogue feels empty and a lot of Melinoe's relationship with others is just "good luck on your quest to kill Chronos we're rooting for you". Maybe this will improve as they add more content and the story evolves a bit more.  Still, the story's pretty good when it kicks off and I'm eager to see where it goes.   In short: Hades 2 is a worthy sequel. There's still some stuff that can (and probably will) improve. That and the fact that the story is incomplete means you should probably wait until release unless you're impatient like me.

text: The video game is good. That's all for that.  Is It Better Than Hades 1.   Okay, that's a great question, that's the real question.   So, Hades 2 is a bigger, wider, harder game with a lot more to do do and discover. Truthfully it is Hades 2 & 3 stuck together. But-- if I'm gonna be so real, I think that Hades 1 is just... better?   Okay, so this is gonna have big spoilers. For everything I guess.  [h1] **SPOILERS** [/h1]  So Hades 1 is this tight really well composed story about a boy and his dad and family and secrets. It's not heady, it's not esoteric, it's classic stuff. The gameplay is quick and snappy. The builds are fun. The zones can be kind of a drag. Elysium is a pain in the ass.   Then Hades 2-- big epic story about you versus Time. CAN TIME NOT BE STOPPED? Then you gotta go to Olympus and FIGHT THE FATHER OF ALL MONSTERS. And it's all this stuff and all these things and its DIRE and SCARY and the tone is VERY dark and Chronos is extremely difficult and-- and then...   And then it just stops?   Then it just... stops.   It just ends. And everyone lives happily every after?  So-- like... yeah, it just..   When you get to the point of Hades 1 where you're hearing "In The Blood" it feels like you've triumphed in so many ways. Your relationship with your family, your dad, you got your mom, your dog... it's so powerful.   And in this one you just.. Well, someone ELSE does stuff and then...?  So, I'll be real, the gameplay is massively improved. The maps are fun. The weapons are different, largely fun. The combat is a bit slower but it feels better. I just don't feel like the story lived up to what I know Supergiant is capable of. This still feels like it's half finished. I don't know. It's worth your time. It's still amazing. It's just... not what it could have been.

text: Hades 2 is one of the best sequels I’ve played in terms of gameplay, but the story’s resolution is so weak it soured the entire experience for me.  As a sequel, it gets almost everything right. Nothing from the original was sacred enough to keep unchanged, yet it still holds true to its roots. The addictive “just one more run” loop is still there. The new weapons are interesting and feel distinct, while the Arcana system is a great evolution of what came before. The Fear system adds challenge and variety, and the boons and keepsakes keep builds fresh and fun to experiment with. The art, music, and voice acting — classic Supergiant polish. Hades 2 is bigger, better, braver.  Where the game falls apart is in the [i]True Ending[/i]. The buildup is strong, but the resolution is unsatisfying, unearned, and undermines the protagonist. Hades 1 worked as a story about family because it leaned into that theme. Hades 2 sets itself up as a story about vengeance — until the finale abruptly discards that in favor of a “family-first” resolution that feels rushed and out of place. Worse, the conclusion strips Melinoë of agency. Her lifelong struggle and growth are brushed aside for a resolution dictated by someone else. She becomes a bystander in her own finale. It doesn’t feel bittersweet or thought-provoking, just hollow. For a studio known for powerful storytelling, this is easily their weakest writing yet.  Death to Chronos.
