text: As someone that played the hell out of the first game and loved it to bits, this game is in an extremely rough state at the moment and needs polishing.   Health from enemies are in dire need of re-tuning. This could probably solve most of the later gripes I will mention later on. It's probably a problem that solves itself by levelling Grasp enough and taking every card imaginable, but realistically if you're not at that point and have a bad run you're just going to be sitting there forever beating on a guy with tons of health. Especially in later areas. And on that note, enemy density is unreasonably through the roof in later areas on top of all their health.  Some of these mobs are also boring to fight if you're being optimal about conserving health.  An example is that the majority of mobs in Erebus have insanely long lasting hitboxes that encourage you to slow play from a distance. No one is jumping into that clusterfuck of vines, spinning lasers and banshees screaming at you and coming out unscathed. Especially with one less dash to work with in this game. Chances are you're going to just set up a Cast and throw shit at them while they're trapped in it. Especially if they have armour.  While Nemesis choosing routes and buying boons before you mid run is a cool worldbuilding touch, it's a lot less amusing when the numbers are currently overtuned and you're already not having a good run for her to run off with your boons. The wager minigame with her isn't that great compared to the first game with Thanatos. She kinda just one shots everything immediately, so running into her in the Fields of Mourning where everything starts to become tanky means you need to have absurd amounts of damage to win.  Getting sent to Asphodel is basically a run ender at the moment. You need to stay in an extremely small circle while a bunch of armored up Inferno Bombers go sicko mode on you. The charge on the circle decreases extremely fast so leaving the circle because you needed to dodge and coming back is sort of a non-option. You don't really get anything awesome out of it either like when you're forced to pick between gods and one gets mad at you in the first game. You just got chosen to be put in an unreasonably hard room early on in your run and now you're going to lose tons of health over it. You might as well die and start over instead of hobbling along.  Boons feel a lot less impactful because they're being watered down by new boons that are forcing me to engage with the clunky, unwieldy Omega system.  Chaos is probably the worst offender of all at the moment. Most of the boons they offer does not at all feel worth the trouble you need to go through to get them, unlike the first game.  Depending on how the laser trap is positioned in Tartarus, you can walk into a room with it immediately touching you and you'll lose health as soon as you can act.  There's a one shot mechanic during the Chronos fight that feels so awful in it's design. Now, if it was extremely obvious how to deal with the mechanic and I failed it anyway, I'd agree it was deserved. But the visual language is such a disaster that there's multiple conclusions you could draw in how to deal with it. And having to experiment on the solution to a one shot mechanic at the end of a 45 minute run is so utterly baffling I can't believe the people that made this made the first Hades.    If you loved the combat in the first game I'd suggest waiting for a bit for them to polish the game to be a little less rough around the edges. If you just want the story, you can probably solve most of the problems mentioned above by turning on God Mode.

text: A pretty alright game that completely fumbles the ending to such a degree that it actively soured the entire experience for me.  The gameplay structure is the same as Hades 1, you collect boons and misc. materials in runs, you do your relationship content between runs, then you do another run, repeat. All well and good except for the part where there are so many additional dialogue triggers per runs that you'll sometimes stack up dozens of conversation variations that might take priority over the ones you actually care about to make progress.  As a mostly spoiler free example, I needed to talk to a boss to trigger a specific conversation for a companion's relationship track in the crossroads. I had 5 other dialogues that took priority and some other quests that involved using heat. Now the boss has to get through all of those and their special heat dialogues, then an ADDITIONAL dialogue for turning off heat. even then, I did not trigger the conversation that was supposed to appear. Repeat that roughly 15 times.  The story was pretty coherent throughout, the characters are fun and interesting until the game suddenly decides that not only does Melinoe not have any agency anymore, nobody does! To make it even better, none of the characters in the game itself understand how the ending works. If you write an ending where every single character involved is as unhappy and confused as the player, is it even a good ending? It's bad to the point where I would love to know if whoever wrote it was normally that misogynistic, or if they just stumbled into it while writing the last few hours of the main story. I don't even want to finish the epilogue for completion's sake.

text: Supergiant Games' Hades 2 is a phenomenal roguelike that, even in its current form, can deliver hundreds of hours of absolute quality entertainment and will leave anyone who gets their hands on it waiting for the full release.  Years have passed since the end of young Zagreus' adventure, and the idyllic picture of hell built by the son of Hades is now completely shattered. The return of Cronus, the father of all the gods who had previously rebelled against Olympus, has led to the devastating defeat of the entire Greek pantheon, whose hopes of victory rest solely on Melinoe, the youngest daughter of the king of hell and immortal princess of the underworld. Hecate, the goddess of magic, miraculously rescued Melinoe while she was still in swaddling clothes and hid her in an area between Olympus and Tartarus, home to dozens of exiles, including the children of Nyx who had escaped the cataclysm. Here, trained by Hecate, the legendary hero Odysseus, Nemesis, the embodiment of vengeance, and other mythical beings, Melinoe becomes the key to a grand and secret plan to overthrow Cronus, the usurper she has hated all her life.  On paper, the mission is apparent. By harnessing the immortality that binds her to the afterlife, Melinoe can repeatedly attempt to reach and destroy the titan of time, returning to the starting point stronger and better prepared than before. With this seemingly simple mechanic, a plot and narrative universe unfolds, significantly expanding the foundation first laid by Hades, involving dozens of characters, from mythical witches like Medea and Circe to figures like Icarus, Narcissus, and Heracles, and finally every god of the Greek pantheon and even many of the most famous mythological monsters. In addition to being extraordinarily characterized, drawn, and voiced, all these characters become the tiles of a narrative mosaic perfectly integrated into the game: every journey, every victory, and every defeat never fails to advance the plot, seamlessly using the roguelike spirit to underpin all aspects of progression.  In keeping with the previous game, Melinoe must choose one of the mythological weapons to embark on this bloody journey. Nevertheless, Supergiant Games has considered all the major criticisms and turned them into unexpected strengths. First of all, the game has many differences that are not limited to aesthetics but also affect the overall structure of the experience: Wide open spaces are encountered. There are small hubs where you can complete specific missions. Sometimes, there are complex vertical arenas. In essence, the overall variety and depth of the maps have been greatly improved. However, the main innovation lies in the protagonist's various paths.  Melinoe not only has to devote herself to the search for Cronus in Tartarus but also fulfills the task of helping Olympus directly in the field. This results in two ever-different main paths, each with unique areas, characters, resources, enemies, and encounters. Where will Melinoe go? To the depths of Erebo or the surface of the fallen city of Ephira? Will Cronus drag her to Asphodel, or will she pass through this side undisturbed? This is just the tip of a massive iceberg of unexpected decisions and events that make each journey different from the last and will only come to full fruition when the early access period ends.  The game's core mechanics are identical to the first game's chapters and outlines. There's no shortage of elements you'd expect to find in any self-respecting roguelike, between the small tasks to complete and the numerous optional modes, many of which are "hardcore." These, in turn, are tied to unique reward chains. But even in this "work-in-progress" version, there is no single element of the previous installment that has not been expanded or deepened. At least the narrative is as central, interactive, and willing to accommodate as many other surprises as ever.  As in the past, the game starts to take shape precisely according to the choices made by the player. Here, the producers have done a great job. They've crafted several new layers of depth by introducing six brand new weapons, each equipped with different variants, several "pets" that provide different aids in battle, a deck of tarot cards that significantly affect Melinoe's abilities, and several valuable tools for gathering resources along the way, which positively adds to many of the mechanics already encountered in the previous game.  The critical difference between Zagreus and Melinoe lies in the girl's mage abilities. These abilities will require a particular mana bar to launch different variants of each available attack - i.e., magically charged moves. These include a magic circle that locks enemies in place, a running attack that blocks an escape attempt by holding down, and a final ability that, this time, isn't tied to individual deities but to interactions with the moon goddess Selene. The choice to separate Melinoe's most potent attack from the list of elemental buffs has resulted in the inclusion of particular skill trees where players can choose from many categories and slowly increase them at a specific rate throughout each game session.  At its core, the game remains an excellent procedural action-based mix of destroying hordes of enemies and facing bosses of increasing difficulty, with the ultimate goal of completing the entire loop in one direction—the difficulty level ramps dramatically, with some fights taking on almost bullet-hell-style overtones. There's no need to fear, though, as there's no obstacle that can be overcome with Melinoe's training and meticulous planning while also adopting an excellent progression system independent of individual trials' progress. In short, this is an improved, expanded, refined, and deeper version of the classic Hades experience, whose formula flows seamlessly.  Obviously, beyond the content, a title as deep and varied as Hades 2 hides a lot of sneaky variables on the balancing front, so it's clear that early access will address that aspect as well. Last time around, work continued for two years before reaching the official launch. Still, it puts Melinoe's adventure in the hands of the public in a way that is nothing short of dazzling, capable of holding interest for hundreds of hours without showing any signs of fatigue. Of course, Supergiant Games' perfectionist nature is what has the studio's name on everyone's lips, and they certainly won't stop adding new meat to the fire. Still, in the unlikely event of a release in 2024, we'll be looking at a serious contender for Game of the Year. So buy this masterpiece and take advantage of the pleasure.

text: Once again another game that delivers on every front. If you liked the first Hades you are gonna fall in love with this one. The easiest way to explain it is just the first game with more in every aspect, more enemies, more dynamic combat, more interactions with characters, its everything that the first game wishes it was. I think the best part is that between how the new combat system works, and the new boons you get from the Gods, that the game feels more dynamic when playing it. The new boons enable new playstyles on established weapons which is refreshing if you've been playing Hades for a while now, but also enable you to get more creative. In the last game it felt like you had to pray a hammer showed up for your build to feel distinct, Hades II new magick bar lets you experiment with each weapon in a way that each run truly feel unique. I believe that even just in its developmental stages Hades II clears the first Hades in sheer gameplay alone, and considering the way the story is laid out right now, that it absolutely will clear the first games narrative when its finished.

text: At first glance you see there is much more, and much better than the first instalment.  Although I highly recommend playing Hades I first, because the story in Hades II grabs you by the neck and hooks you immensely. For the little I've seen there are recurring characters, you revisit places from the first one, and a huge enigma and catastrophe has happened between the two games, which you unearth bit by bit. All that tension and engagement is lost if you haven't played the first one, just like the enjoyment you feel when seeing again characters you are familiar with from the first game.  Also, it is considerably more complicated, convoluted even, and hard. I know for a fact that in the long run, once I understand more the game, those are great news and pleasure to be had. Thankfully many mechanics I am very accustomed to from the first game, and that doesn't become a problem. I don't think new players would find Hades II as enjoyable.  For many reasons, these two games are a must. They are some of the best made and written in recent times. The replayability is unbelievable. And the developers are incredibly generous. Long after unlocking all achievements, there is still a lot of content to unlock, and the players are not punished by crazy and insane achievements even though the content goes far beyond them.  Hades is one of the most pleasant discoveries I've ever had in gaming, and I can't see myself stop playing them for a long, long, very long time.  Go kill Time  And see you in Hell

text: While Hades 2 retains the mechanical fun of its predecessor, it stumbles in nearly every other aspect that made the original special.  The boon system feels frustratingly unbalanced, lacking the carefully tuned synergies that made build-crafting satisfying in the first game. More critically, the progression loop has lost its edge—the grind that once felt rewarding now feels hollow and unrewarding. Where Hades kept you coming back for "one more run," Hades 2 struggles to justify the repetition.  The narrative is where this sequel truly falters. The original told a powerful story about hope, tolerance, and family reconciliation that resonated emotionally. Hades 2 trades that uplifting journey for something far less inspiring—you slog through hell only to arrive at an underwhelming "meh" of a conclusion. The story also suffers from misogynistic undertones and feels disappointingly half-baked, as if the writers couldn't commit to a cohesive vision.  Despite moment-to-moment gameplay that can still entertain, Hades 2 fails to capture the heart and soul of what made its predecessor a masterpiece. The weak progression, poor narrative payoff, and problematic story elements make it hard to recommend, especially to fans hoping for more of what made Hades great.

text: As a huge fan of the original Hades (with hundreds of hours spread out over my console and PC) I was extremely excited when Supergiant Games announced in 2022 that they were doing a sequel. With bated breath I waited for more news and then in 2024 it launched and I started the install remotely so it would be ready to play.   Setting aside the fact that this is still an EARLY ACCESS and therefore unfinished game, Hades fans going into this game may expect or even want it to be the same as the original. After all, we have spent hundreds of hours running around as Zagreus and getting our timings down for each boss. Hades II takes all that was established in Hades I and evolves it. It forces players to try new styles and pacing of fighting allowing them to take the skills they earned as Zagreus and apply them to Melinoe and vice versa. I have LOVED figuring out each weapon and then when a patch comes out I get to learn them all again as they have been tuned and improved.   The overall gameplay is familiar to fans. Go out, fight enemies, get boons, die a lot, repeat.  The game is filled with both old and new faces for you to interact with (I'm looking at you [spoiler]Bouldy[/spoiler]) unique weapons, powers, etc. All in all it is a ton of fun to play and I am deeply enjoying the early access process while at the same time getting further hyped up for the full release ([spoiler]Chronos is too cocky for his own good...I need to destroy him[/spoiler])  But for me what has always stood out to me and set Supergiant above most other game developers is the care and research that they have put into developing their characters. The little details that give little tidbits of each legendary character (Hermes and his turtle, all of Chaos, [spoiler]Narcissus, Hephestus (seriously amazing character design)[/spoiler], Aphrodite, etc, etc.) I can go on and on about each one and not just their character art, but their lines, and interactions with each other. My history nerd is extremely happy.   This game is a work of art and is a worthy successor to Hades I. I cannot wait to play the the full release! Great job Supergiant!

text: The game is great, with fantastic character art and the storylines are amazing. Really gripping and worth every penny. The looping is smooth and very addictive, the mystery feels surreal, the voice acting is great and all the little mini games you can do are fun. Progress feels linear and rewarding, making the gameplay loop amazing.  Only gripe is the storyline. Melinoe is too perfect, too goodie-two shoes and lacks some of the grit Zagreus had which made him fun. You hardly relate to Melinoe. Sure she can be naive at times and endearing but for a protagonist we live through so long, she is tiresome. Especially the end made me not root for her anymore.   Spoiler re story beats I highly disliked: [spoiler]The ending story-line falls short. We do not even see Hades and Persephone in the House, we hardly see Zagreus, she is not reunited with her family at all. It is just fighting and war, ever-ongoing for her. It is so unsatisfying. I wish we visually saw the accomplishments we fought to achieve: a safe Olympus and a restored House of Hades.  I wish we saw more of the Olympus drama as a reward for beating the last Olympus boss, I wish we saw more of the House of Hades cast as a lil reward for beating Chronos. But nope. I feel like they could have come up with a different solution as to why we can keep playing the game, like she needs to continue training or something.   The found family of the Crossroads feels really flat. Why can't they all go to the House of Hades? Replacing that as your starter area after the epilogue could've been cool. Or having Hades/Zag/whoever else from her family visit from time to time at least. The fact that our protagonist, after her whole story, is rewarded with continuous "work" instead of being surrounded by the people she fought to save is lame. No one from the Crossroads -feels- like found family. Just war comrades and unserious romantic interests. [/spoiler]

text: Combat gameplay has much more variety and is way better than the first game. There's no denying that.  My only real issue is the story.  It's so convoluted and you spend dozens of hours grinding character storylines and prophecies. If you don't have the luxury to go in completely blind, you'll probably end up looking up guides because some prophecies require talking to specific characters in a specific order. That makes it very easy to accidentally spoil yourself, so by the time you reach the epilogue, it has the emotional impact of a wet noodle.  Another problem is that the "true" ending is locked behind an excessive amount of grinding. The game itself isn't that long. Its playtime is artificially extended by making you farm items and exhaust dialogue.  By the time I finally unlocked the real ending, I was completely burned out. Instead of feeling motivated to experiment with builds or push higher Fear like I did in Hades 1, I just wanted to stop playing. The ending felt more like relief than a reward.  And my biggest problem is the context of the normal ending, Chronos. The fact that he suddenly becomes good after being bombarded with false memories from an alternate timeline feels like a rushed ending to his story and a plot device pulled out of thin air. The villain who literally kidnapped and imprisoned half of your family members in time and ate his own children is suddenly a kind and loving grandfather. The game doesn't do nearly enough to earn his redemption. At the end the phrase "Death to Chronos" lost it's meaning completely.  But all in all, the game is quite fun if you focus on the gameplay, that being the main attraction of the game, and it's an absolute must play if you liked the first installment.

text: Great game. I started with Hades so I'll use this review to compare Hades II to the original.  Gameplay: Hades II has an edge. The weapons and aspects are an improvement, the Arcana Card system is flexible, and the wide variety of boons make a for ton of fun and viable builds. Hades II also has a more carefully thought out reward system. It's possible to progress further in Hades II without as much of the relentless grinding that's needed in Hades.  Story: Hades was superior to Hades II in this regard. Zagreus is a substantially more intriguing character than Melinoë. The central story of Hades is more touching, with a far better conclusion. While Hades II offers a broader cast, many of the additional characters add little to the experience. The epilogue was particularly lackluster.

text: I really wish I could recommend this game, but to put it kindly and vaguely there is no amount of improved gameplay mechanics or stunning art direction/music tracks or charming characters that can save this game from its horrid ending. So, so much potential. Almost all of it thrown away for an ending that felt rushed and questionable at best, and like it was outright punishing the player and protagonist at worst. I really did love this game once. I've been playing since day one early access and I have spent the past year and a half blown away by its potential and storytelling. I just can't understand how they threw all of it away and wrote an ending that made all of it feel so meaningless. Sucked all of the joy straight out of it. It's not fun anymore. Dare I say it even begins to stain the legacy of the franchise. At least the original actually felt like it had heart. Why play a game where all of my actions feel undermined from beginning to end? Why care about the protagonist when her actions and decisions and opinions will never matter? How do you frame this as a happy end? How can you mischaracterize your own characters so badly? How did you manage to make those who were previously so beloved suddenly unlikeable and unrecognizable as themselves?  This game could have easily been GOTY had it not been for its ending. The hours of gameplay building up to it will not feel worth it or rewarding in any way. Save your time and money.

text: Hades II is still in Early Access at the time of writing this review, but I still want to share my opinion on the game so far.  I have been waiting for around 4 years for the release of Hades II after having played Hades I for around 200 hours, and I can tell you, as a player who is normally picky about the smallest details, this game WILL NOT disappoint you.  Although many people still criticize the game for being pretty much the same as Hades I and not being all that different from its predecessor, I would say I both agree and disagree with that statement.  While the game shares the same concept and core idea as the first one, the development team really listens to the community. They implement new changes and add features recommended by the player base, which I find extremely commendable. You don’t often find many creators who do that sort of thing, especially considering that Supergiant Games is a relatively small company without the unlimited resources that larger studios have.  On the other hand, shouldn’t the game resemble the first one, since it is its successor and continuation? I understand the public’s remarks, but I still think it makes sense for Hades II to stick to its original foundational concepts, just with new Gods, questlines, regions, bosses, etc.  In the end, I am glad that the team not only listens to its community but also stays true to the concept of the first game.  In summary, I’d like to make a small table of things I REALLY LIKED and things that might still need improvement.  PROS:  THE SOUNDTRACKS – This is probably the best part of the entire game, and I don’t mean that in a negative way regarding everything else. The music is just reaaaaally good. The Mechanics – While they haven’t been completely overhauled, there are still quite a lot of changes to the mechanics, and I am fond of them. The Art Style – As always, no game from Supergiant disappoints when it comes to art style. The Gameplay – With such a wide variety of choices—boons, hammers, arcane cards, pets, weapons, weapon arts—the game could hardly ever get boring. The Amount of Personas – The number of NPCs in the game is just HUGE, and I find it extremely intriguing to meet and explore their personalities and questlines, hear their voices, and admire their designs. The Price – The price is so good for a game of this quality that I honestly think it should cost more to better reflect the team’s efforts.  CONS:  The Mobs – Maybe the only thing I am not particularly fond of is the mob spawn rate and the mobs themselves. It feels quite unfair in some stages, such as Mount Olympus or Tartarus, where 1,000 mobs are constantly spawning with insane attacks and attack patterns. One example of a completely UNFAIR mob would be the Dracon. This mini-boss gave me a harder time than Prometheus or even the God of Time himself! Nevertheless, I hope and believe they will make some changes to this in future updates.  With all that said, I conclude that the game is AMAZING. I can only encourage people to BUY and PLAY this game, and I hope it wins one of the GAME OF THE YEAR AWARDS for 2024!

my plants, and check on aspect progress, and weigh all of that against which tool i need to bring, and the idea that i need to finish an entire run before i can get any resources from another tool makes me wanna bury myself alive. its too managey and i dont want that. maybe thats inherently my problem, but i wouldnt be bothered if i didnt feel like i was shooting myself in the foot via opportunity cost CONSTANTLY. the nagging feeling that i could literally abandon my run for the sake of snagging the resources i already got and being able to save my literal human time in reality to further my 'progress' when i already know the run isnt looking insanely good. how much is that time worth to me?   i dont know if i wish it was more like hades 1, or if it had iterated further on the concepts and divorced itself from the initial formula, but in my eyes the game is an crooked bastardization of a handful of really cool and interesting concepts awkwardly smashed together. the strange balance between lore/story and gameplay leaves BOTH to be more desired for me. i want either more story or let me continue to have a chance at making real progress in the video game i paid 30 bucks for.  if you liked hades 1 youll probably like it enough to squeeze a reasonable amount of gameplay from it and maintain a warm fuzzy feeling for the lovely people at supergiant

text: One of those increasingly rare moments where an Early Access is actually worth it!  Beyond expectations. If you liked Hades, you will likely love this sequel  The art style, writing, and narration are fantastic, as one would expect from Supergiant's games. text: This is a game of "If you know, you'll love!'  Newcomers, head my words.  Play Hades I.  You must.  It is fine tuned and perfect.  It will build a love within you, if you give it the time. Wonderful!    At the time of writing this review, the combat is great, by Tartarus even, fantastic, but I feel a bit sluggish.  Maybe I haven't found the rhythm, the right combination of cards, boons, or maybe these veteran fingers were broken trying to escape from Hades the FIRST (read thousandth) time.  Melinoe just doesn't seem to have the familiar zip that Zagreus had.  She is a new character and I may just have to learn in time (read as wait for updates and die a lot), but that's the only flaw.    Well done dev team.  This tortured soul cannot wait to see what gifts you bring to the table.

text: Feels silly to mark the game as not recommended, given I have over 100 hours in it, but Steam only gives a binary option for the score, and on balance, I think the sequel is Supergiant's first real misfire.  Mechanically, it's fine - the tuning is on point, there's variety of equally viable options, the meta-progression works. However, it's a textbook more-of-the-same follow up. You mix and match the boons, you unlock and power up the weapons, and you gift nectar & ambrosia to a bunch of characters to fill up their relationship bars. There's a few different power-up boards, and a wider variety of resources, and the new character has a different move set, but - absent a couple of inconsequential mini-games - you don't do anything that actually feels new. It's just more Hades.  But that would all be fine if the story was good. After all, the big reason behind Hades' success was the perfect mix of gameplay and narrative - a story-heavy roguelike, with a story that could only work in a roguelike. A fun spin on Greek mythos, with refreshingly low stakes and refreshingly messy cast of characters. And hitting certain milestones - first completion, 10th completion, the true ending - added a new, sensible, enjoyable spin on the tale. It really worked.  The story in Hades II, unfortunately, hits none of those marks for me.  It starts off generic. There's a big, bad, ancient evil that took over Underworld and besieged Mount Olympus, and you are the last, best hope of the resistance. Your character is very driven and very serious. The secondary cast in her camp is mostly very driven and very serious. You have many conversations about your very important, world-saving mission. You largely abhor fun, as it gets in the way of saving the world. Both the stakes and the relationships have been established long in the past, and they barely shift as you play. And then you hit the credits - the certain-number-of-completions part - and it goes wildly off the rails. Not only is the ending itself bad, it breaks the rest of the narrative from here on out. If you have old conversations queued up, they no longer make sense. The new dialogues, trying to contextualise what you currently do, are gobbledygook. And then something similar happens with essentially all the side stories, and the true ending - what was once presented as a very serious storyline either goes for a flat comedy ending, or just tapers off mid-sentence, without any payoff whatsoever.  There's a few minor characters that are still messy fun, and they are - without a fail - either unaware of, or uninterested in the overarching story. Best example of that is anyone you'd meet as a second boss. The early part of the game, and the mystery of who the next boss will be, is the game at its best. Fighting those bosses, figuring out where they fit into the story, and figuring out best weapons and buffs, is what kept me entertained long after I checked out from the narrative. The one-more-run loop still largely works. It's objectively a decent game, and I can see myself jumping back in for another run here & there.  So why not recommend it? Because there's a good chance it will disappoint you, even if you're someone that played and loved the first Hades. And if you haven't played the first Hades, you should absolutely go play that instead.

text: One of the greatest sequels ever made, the inclusion of 2 separate routes and the refinements made to the core gameplay make this a must play for every fan of the original game.  My main point of criticism is that the climax of the story doesn't land the same way it did in the original but the game more than makes up for this by introducing a more interesting set of supporting characters. Hades II is bigger, faster, more challenging, arguably prettier and better sounding than the original Hades and a monumental achievement for Supergiant Games.  If you enjoyed the original or action roguelites in general don't think twice before grabbing this, you won't regret it.

text: The top rated review says it's harder than the first. I don't know what it's on about, because I've had an easier time. I can credit some of that to the hours I put into the first game, but there are some early access balance issues I think actually make the game less difficult. There is more at your disposal to help you, and some boons are honestly too overpowered (looking at you Hephaestus). It took around 15 hours to beat the first boss. Now that I'm at 40 hours, I'm starting to run out of things to do (but that only hypes me for the full release). This doesn't mean it's not a challenging and difficult roguelike, but everything I've said here is contradictory to the "it's too hard" top review. It's easier than the first, there are actually more tools to help, things don't take any longer to unlock, and I've already cleared it multiple times now.  The first Hades was easily in my top roguelikes, and my most played new game of that year. This will be just as good when it's out of early access, because it's already so good where it is now. It might even be better. Props to the devs. This is why I've abandon AAA titles for the indie devs, they actually care about their player base before their profits.  [edit: I'm sorry. PLEASE make Chaos otherworldly and perplexed by humans again, not cosplaying as them. And smaller complaint but why does Dio, the soft cozy guy, have hard edges, while Artemis, the hard-ass sharp shooter, is soft and cozy looking?[/spoiler] luv u supergiant]

text: Finally some Hades again! I was almost addicted to the first game and couldnt wait for another serving, once i heard about it. And Hades 2 doesnt really disappoint. Hades 2 is in its world, characters and gameplay features almost twice as big as Hades 1. The new weapons, the inclusion of Magick, new bosses and the new Arcana cards are an interesting and innovative try to keep the gameplay loop fresh and to not copy the first game step-by-step. So that is a great plus. And they achieved just that. Combat also feels great and just as snappy as the first game.   I do have some caveats though. First, they didnt want to copy the mechanics of certain Olympian gods from the first game. I get that. But some gods' boons just feel so..... characterless. In the first game, i knew exactly in what direction certain Olympian boons would take me. In Hades 2 many of them just feel so mushy. It is hard to explain... Second, not only have the world and the features doubled in quantity, but also the amount of collectable resources, upgradeable items and their requirement to unlock stuff. The grind is far worse than in Hades 1. Three, i finished the story in 1.0 and it felt rushed, incomplete and weird. There were quite a few narrative holes. They tried to fix that and did fix it to a good degree in the most recent patch as of writing this review, but to me that was a big no-no. Dont release your game as finished when you have such a directionless story. That was very uncharacteristic of Supergiant. And i am not the only one. I scoured many forums like Steam and Reddit, where also a decent number of people expressed their consternation about that original ending. Four, the relationships between the characters sometimes feel either forced or shallow or both. Especially the romantic ones. Exceptions apply, of course. text: After already being a big fan of the first one, which I purchased after the full launch, I was very excited for the sequel. I usually don't buy a game during early access for various reasons, lack of content and polish and some bad experiences just being some reasons, but with Hades 2 I don't regret it at all. Sure, there are some placeholders for several characters, there might be some maps missing (I'm assuming, my runs seem pretty complete actually), but nothing gamebreaking, no bugs as far as I can tell and most if not all important mechanics to enjoy the gameplay are completely realized.  Honestly might be the most finished early access title I have played so far. It already feels like it delivers more content than the 1.0 of its predecessor and there's still more to come.  I especially love the way they are telling a story, which rogue-likes usually lack because of the gameplay loop, but the way Hades 2 does it (just like Hades 1) works perfectly.  There is a bit of a learning curve but it's really not too steep. Their are a lot of things to unlock, which happens at a pleasant pace (you're neither going to feel like hitting a wall repeatedly but also you won't feel extremely overpowered early on).  Overall this is just a really well made game with a lot of mechanics that interact with each other very well. Easy to learn, hard to master, and so far it manages to be fun the whole way through. I can undertsand everyone wanting to wait for the 1.0 and that's reasonable, but if you are interested in this game and are only holding back because of early access - just buy it now, it's already a very good game and it will probably only get better with time.

text: [h2] A Premium Godlike [/h2]  Ever since The Binding of Isaac I've been chasing the dopamine rush that so many rougelikes seek to recreate but for me, few manage to do.   Hades 2 provides that sense of discovery and experimentation that I adore and is bolstered by satisfying base building and unmatched presentation.  The gameplay builds upon the first game with a more varied moveset, a plethora of weapons and even things like [spoiler] familiars [/spoiler] that can have a big impact on the way you play. Each boon feels impactful and by design there are avenues available to really drill down into a certain playstyle. It's cliche but no two runs are the same (much like Isaac) and taking a risk on that new passive or power only to turn it into a broken, unstoppable run just feels so good.  Then there's the downtime between runs which you can spend upgrading and expanding. It may sound simple but it's such an innate, pleasing feeling to tick off checkboxes and fill up progress bars to then be rewarded with passive upgrades, visual alterations like new decorations or even whole new areas. Base building is nothing original but in Hades 2 it's woven so masterfully into the gameplay loop that it reinforces that "one more run" fixation you can easily slip into.  Tying it all together is of course the unparalleled art, presentation and sound design. The game is pure beauty to play through, the environments, weapon effects and character designs are all top tier and really go a long way to enhance the experience. The voice acting was very impressive, mostly in the fact that I was still hearing new lines every run and the quality in how these lines were delivered were enough to make me think "woah this is good voice acting" and I know nothing about voice acting.  The soundtrack is vast and varied, meets the tone in every situation and ultimately just slaps, there are some real bangers in here.  You may have heard that the ending lets this game down, and I would have to agree. Honestly, the gameplay is so strong I thought the narrative would play second fiddle and be relatively inconsequential to my playthrough but the execution of the ending fell so flat and sudden that for a moment, I felt little motivation to push on.  This passed relatively quickly, and although I like the [i] idea [/i] of the ending I just feel it could have been implemented better, maybe built towards a little more gradual. However it is worth noting that there is substantial post-game content available here after the credits roll and some fun story threads to follow.  Anyway, for me that does little to take away from what an incredible game this is and a superb sequel that builds upon the first game in nearly every way.

text: What a slog.  [spoiler] I grinded out 40 some odd hours for a shit ending where Chronos engages in the most violently abrupt heel turn ever witnessed in the medium: going from Dr. Claw to doting, toothless Grandpa with nary a warning. Patch in as many new endings as you want, Supergiant, it doesn't change the fact that Chrono Trigger has no arc to justify said turn. To make it even more delectable, let's throw in some alternate timeline/multiverse mumbo jumbo to be the justification for why you have to keep doing runs and keep this milquetoast witch away from being with the family she's been deprived of and has been training HER ENTIRE LIFE TO SAVE, so she can hang out in her underground bungalow with the rest of the coven. Grind out another almost 30 hours to find The Fates, only to be met with some gender swapped Three Stooges schtick, before just as quickly being told to fuck off and leave them be. And just when you think things couldn't get any more insulting, that multiverse/alternate timeline junk you kids can't seem to get enough of comes back for what I'm gonna dub a brief, second epilogue, where it's revealed that your foster mom is actually YOU. RIVETING. STUNNING. GROUNDBREAKING STUFF. GIVE THESE GUYS AND GALS ANOTHER HUGO. 5 AND A HALF STARS OUT OF 5.[/spoiler]  Is there a mountain of effort and meticulous detail on display in every facet of this work from voice acting to music to art design to writing, etc.? Of course there is. But that doesn't automatically make this an overall enjoyable experience. Unlike Hades 1, I was [i]praying[/i] for this thing to end. Your emotional investment comes not from strong characterization of Melinoë and seeing her overcome her struggles, but from saving the guy from the first game that you actually [i]liked[/i]. Melinoë is the definition of a Mary Sue: prim, proper, always level headed, never makes mistakes, utterly boring. The writers have placed her in a bubble and refuse to burden her character with any flaws or deficiencies that might make her feel relatable and real. As for the combat, it's like the first game but two or three steps down. That said, I can empathize with this point at least; you already worked through the stock weapon types while doing the first game to the point where you had to add a fucking gun by the end of it, so sure, add a goddamn jetpack and that skull weapon that I wouldn't touch with a 50 foot pole to fill out the sequel's armory. While I was complaining for the first few runs, I, and I'm assuming 95% of people who play past the first few hours, will just get used to all the new quirks and find a go to weapon.   Despite all it has going for it, Hades 2 never feels like it justifies its existence. It's Hades 1 but MORE™ and worse.

text: It is shocking to see that Hades 2 is only in early access, and that Supergiant Games plans to let it spend at least the rest of 2024 there before it’s ready to call it version 1.0. Shocking, because it already has just about everything I want from a sequel to one of the best roguelite action games of all time. Hades 2 manages to keep everything that made the original such a masterclass of design, but it does so in a way that changes up how each of the pieces fits together and gives it its own unique identity rather than feeling like a glorified expansion. The result is a familiar, but fresh follow up that challenged, surprised, and delighted me with every triumph and failure in equal measure. There are a few things missing, with an actual ending to its story being the most substantial among them, but once it’s complete it’s hard to imagine Hades 2 not living up to the mythological legacy of the first.  I’m not going to spend too long explaining why what’s carried over from the original Hades works so well. IGN gave it our Game of the Year Award in 2020 for a reason, and if you haven’t played the Greek gods’ gift to gamers yet and think you might enjoy some of the smoothest, most stylish isometric action ever made, tied up with a story that just keeps getting deeper with each run, you absolutely should before jumping into round two. I’ll wait.

text: I only got into this Hades last year, so I don't have a ton of history with it. But I greatly enjoyed the first game, I spent 180+ hours enjoying the story, the gameplay and getting to know all the different characters and their stories, so much so that I felt sad when I decided my time with the game was over.  Now I've reached the same point with Hades 2 and there's both relief and sorrow for "finishing" the game. This sequel is as worth of being a sequel to an incredible game as you're going to get, I cannot stress this enough. There's a lot of discourse about this or that and how the first Hades is better, I diisagree with most of that, Hades 2 is simply different in many ways and it tells a different story, while the story of the first is more relateable I find that I enjoyed both almost as much I would say.  My favorite thing about Hades 2 is the combat which in my opinion is head and shoulders above Hades 1, here you can have so many builds and synergies between all the different boons that it still surprises me, often you won't even get a duo boon yet you still melt everything in your path when you find the right build. In Hades 1 you felt like a wet noodle if you didn't find the exact boons and the duo boon to go with them, often the rng didn't give a crap and you struggled with the bosses. Here they did a tremendous job balancing all the different boons and things you could do with them, I can't remember the last time I wore one of the god's keepsakes, they are utterly unnecessary. And to me that is the best and most fun aspect of this game.   I enjoyed the characters so much, they are different, especially Meli, I found that getting to know them and learn more about them made them more fun and interesting, not to mention the voice acting alone made me want to listen to every single line of dialogue they had. SGG never disappoints when it comes to characters and story telling. I did miss a couple of bonds so I could complete my funko pop collection but I'm okay with that for now, I'll get them later so I can feel fully at peace.   Just like with Hades 1, you find yourself unlocking and discovering new things at a perfect pace, the game just keeps growing and giving you more options and things to enjoy the more you play and just when you feel like you've seen everything the game is like "Hey how about this? hope you like it" and you end up having a blast. I just finished my last run to complete my last achievement, the Echo and Narcissus achievement and man, the aspect of moros is so op, at first I wasn't crazy about it cause it worked different from Meli's torches but once you learn how to use it, it's a blast to blow up everything with them. All of the weapons are fun to use if you spend enough time with them, I find the black coat to be the oddest one but I've had some amazing runs with it and I had a blast.   If you don't know wether to play this or Hades 1, start with the first, you won't regret it, both are intimately linked and you will enjoy the story a lot more if you play both in order. But I greatly enjoyed the first game, I spent 180+ hours enjoying the story, the gameplay and getting to know all the different characters and their stories, so much so that I felt sad when I decided my time with the game was over.  Now I've reached the same point with Hades 2 and there's both relief and sorrow for "finishing" the game. This sequel is as worth of being a sequel to an incredible game as you're going to get, I cannot stress this enough. There's a lot of discourse about this or that and how the first Hades is better, I diisagree with most of that, Hades 2 is simply different in many ways and it tells a different story, while the story of the first is more relateable I find that I enjoyed both almost as much I would say.  My favorite thing about Hades 2 is the combat which in my opinion is head and shoulders above Hades 1, here you can have so many builds and synergies between all the different boons that it still surprises me, often you won't even get a duo boon yet you still melt everything in your path when you find the right build. In Hades 1 you felt like a wet noodle if you didn't find the exact boons and the duo boon to go with them, often the rng didn't give a crap and you struggled with the bosses. Here they did a tremendous job balancing all the different boons and things you could do with them, I can't remember the last time I wore one of the god's keepsakes, they are utterly unnecessary. And to me that is the best and most fun aspect of this game.   I enjoyed the characters so much, they are different, especially Meli, I found that getting to know them and learn more about them made them more fun and interesting, not to mention the voice acting alone made me want to listen to every single line of dialogue they had. SGG never disappoints when it comes to characters and story telling. I did miss a couple of bonds so I could complete my funko pop collection but I'm okay with that for now, I'll get them later so I can feel fully at peace.   Just like with Hades 1, you find yourself unlocking and discovering new things at a perfect pace, the game just keeps growing and giving you more options and things to enjoy the more you play and just when you feel like you've seen everything the game is like "Hey how about this? hope you like it" and you end up having a blast. I just finished my last run to complete my last achievement, the Echo and Narcissus achievement and man, the aspect of moros is so op, at first I wasn't crazy about it cause it worked different from Meli's torches but once you learn how to use it, it's a blast to blow up everything with them. All of the weapons are fun to use if you spend enough time with them, I find the black coat to be the oddest one but I've had some amazing runs with it and I had a blast.   If you don't know wether to play this or Hades 1, start with the first, you won't regret it, both are intimately linked and you will enjoy the story a lot more if you play both in order. I know I had alot of fun completing both games which is something I didn't really bother with till I played Hades 1, both are worth playing, enjoying and even completing if that's your thing.

text: [h1]Death to Chronos![/h1]  Hades II is the long-awaited sequel to Hades, and manages to deliver a unique experience while also expanding on basically every aspect of the framework of its predecessor.   The game falls into the rogue-lite genre once again, allowing players to progress the story and character relationships bit by bit with every single run while also giving them the oppertunity to upgrade their arsenal and build a little bit each time, therefore allowing players to reach further and further with each run.  The most notable aspect that got extended is the sheer size of the game. While Hades 1 was already a fairly vast game, Hades II one-ups it in basically all categories. This time there are two routes to conquer instead of a single one - each with its own set of unique enemies, traps, bosses and so on. There are more gods, more boons, more characters, more keepsakes and so many other things to be discovered.  This allows for runs to feel much more unique and varied this time around. Between the weapon aspects, boon combinations and build variations you end up getting runs that feels completely different from each other instead of just falling into the same patterns over and over.  A big chunk of the combat system got revamped with the second game. Instead of using Zagreus' Mirror of Night, Melinoë has access to Arcana Cards, with unique effects that come with various activation costs and trigger conditions, which makes for some inventive builds.  Every attack now also comes with a stronger Omega version that requires Magick to be charged. Using enough Magick also allows you to cast powerful hexes, which are basically this game's version of the god calls from the first game. These new features make the fights feel more fluent and allow players to get much more creative in their approaches.  Of course the game also retains - and improves - basically all the features that made the first game such an outstanding one, from the great soundtrack, to the witty character dialogues, to the customization and decoration options.   Furthermore you can now recruit and customize animal companions, further extend the hub to relax in between runs, tackle various unique trials provided by Chaos, test your skills at the Oath of the Unseen (this game's version of the Pact of Punishment) and so much more.  Overall, if you enjoyed the first Hades game, are a fan of roguelikes/lites - or simply enjoy games with great atmosphere, storytelling and fluent fast-paced mechanics in general, then I wholeheartedly recommend Hades II to you.

text: [POST-RELEASE REVIEW] So what do I think after the full release is finally out? Hmm, I think I hoped for more in the way of the story and character development... I can't honestly say either are anywhere near as strong as the first game. However, is the game fun? It's fun as hell! (Pun unintentional, but approved.)  ===[SHORT REVIEW]===  Honestly, this feels like the perfect sequel: it doesn't replace or invalidate the first game, which I 100% still think everyone should play, but if you have totally beaten the first game and you're yearning for more, this is perfect. Did you start finding the previous battle system a little too simple, and wish that there were more than a few attacks that reward timing? Did you wish there were more area/crowd control mechanics for all those mobs? Well, in that case, you're gonna love this! Yeah, the story is not as good, and the side characters are mostly not as interesting, but it's a sequel, so that's pretty normal. They're still objectively awesome, just not as good as the first game, and that's kinda what I want. It makes me sad when a sequel basically replaces the first game and makes it pointless to play it again, and that's very much not the case here... Instead, Hades 1 & 2 are two halves of an awesome roguelite ARPG whole, and I love them both.  ===[LONG REVIEW]===  Weak story aside, this game's art, music, and gameplay are top notch. I love most of the new god portraits. They've all changed in theme from "gods at rest" to "gods at war", all equipped with armor and weapons, and that's really fun to see. Ares is in his element and I gotta say I sort of love him in this game, where in the previous one I found him mildly creepy. Obviously, the guy's just at his best when an actual war is on. He's surprisingly chill and philosophical about it. I think you get the idea in the previous game that he's a low-key serial killer just itching for war and killing, but when war actually comes, he doesn't seem HAPPY about it, more... satisfied? Engaged? Like "Cool, I finally have something to do!" and I appreciate that.  I suppose the fact that I think Dionysus has the weakest new portrait (although it is extremely hilarious, which was probably the idea) is kind of on theme as well since his godly power of partying is at its weakest at a serious time like war.  I loved every one of the new gods (Selene, Hestia, Hephaestus, Apollo) and all the new boons are interesting and add tons of new strategies to the game. Speaking of the gameplay: how is it, and how does it compare to the first game? Well, as some people have complained, it's more complicated for sure. There are a few melee-type builds where you can just charge in and button-mash to your heart's content, but on the whole, Melinoe requires more strategy to play as.  Personally, I consider that to be a good thing. I love that the cast (Zag's least useful category of attack) has been redone from "throwing a rock" to "awesome area control mechanism." It can hold enemies in place for charged "omega" attacks (which now exist, effectively doubling attack types), and allows you to temporarily protect yourself from melee attacks (and accordingly, I feel like there are a lot more projectiles in this game, though I might be imagining that). It's a really strong mechanic and I love it. I was thinking of replaying the first game because I miss the characters and environments, but honestly, I am not nearly as excited about returning to the previous battle system... it's not that it's not still fun (it is!) but the new system is better and feels like it has wider variety.  How about the new side characters? Eh, they're fine. I like them. Moros is a sweet guy, Nemesis is the tsundere who starts out hostile and comes to respect you, and Dora is hilarious. Odysseus is amazing and why don't we get way more of him?! I was surprised that the writers chose Icarus for image rehabilitation, but good for him, I guess! And as someone who had just listened to all 4 of Stephen Fry's "Mythos" audiobooks (HIGHLY RECOMMENDED), I enjoyed seeing Supergiant's take on the various witches (Hecate, Medea, Circe). I do feel like Prometheus, the champion of humanity, kinda got done dirty, but I guess that's par for the course for the poor guy.  How about the main character? Well... Melinoe is not as likable as Zag, straight up. There's no help for it... serious people are just not as likable as fun people, that's just something that's true in life. However, I respect her and think she's awesome, and that's almost as good! I read a complaint essay a few weeks ago where someone was moaning that it's unfair that as a female character, she's forced to fulfill some kind of business-mom stereotype of being no fun, but I think that person missed the (to me) obvious thing: Zagreus takes after their mom, Persephone, who is forgiving and sweet and nurturing and fun and creative.  Melinoe, however, despite LOOKING more like Persephone, is very much her father's daughter. Super serious, super duty-bound, super set in her beliefs and behaviors. Has difficulty changing her perspective after she's decided something. Powerful emotions buried extremely deeply. She only loses control of her temper with two people in the entire game: Eris, the world's most annoying tsundere (which makes sense, because organized people like Hades and Melinoe find actual Chaos to be the worst thing ever), and Zagreus, her brother, which is kind of sweet.  Anyway, in conclusion: should you play this game? Well, if you loved the first one and wished the battle system were a bit more complex... then yes. Can you play this without playing the first game? I mean... you COULD, but I would not recommend it. The story is much weaker, and also relies on the events of the first game. There are tons and tons of subtle references to the first game (like our favorite Good Shade) that you just won't get, and that's sad. Don't do it! Really, if you play Hades 1 and you DON'T want to immediately get the sequel, I don't think we can be friends.   ===[EARLY-ACCESS REVIEW]=== Currently the game's in early access, but honestly, if you liked the first one, you will definitely want this one. It's more of the same, except different! New characters, new story, new weapons, new boons, new passive abilities, new side bs to do, new decorations you don't need, new environments... all of them of the same high quality as the first game... what's not to love?! It's not even done and it's already my game of whatever year it comes out!

text: When it comes to most talked about games from 2025, I feel like this game went a bit under the radar, especially when compared to other award worthy, big game releases. But from everything I've heard, I knew that the reception to this game was very positive so in 2026 I finally decided to take the plunge and give it a try (I've never played Hades 1 before).  67 hours later I can confidently say that it's such an enjoyable, polished game. I accidentally found myself playing it for 12 hours straight on a Saturday. Every time you think you've seen it all, the game unlocks more small features and gameplay tweaks that make you go "Oh, I can do one more run" and just repeat that forty times until you finally make yourself look at the clock and realize you have work in the morning.  I did play a bit of Transistor back in the day and I know that Supergiant Games have awesome soundtracks and Hades II is no different. The boss battle music is just absolutely top notch. There's this one particular song in the game that just topped Raphael's song from Baldur's Gate 3. It's Disney villain-esque without sounding corny. It frustrates you at first and then you realize it's kind of a banger.  Oh and I absolutely understand why it got the award for best game on Steam deck. Literally the only difference between playing on a monitor and playing on Steam deck is that you have a bigger screen on a monitor. The game runs at a consistent 90 FPS, it's not a battery killer like some games and the controls are comfortable in your hand because you're not having to adjust the in-game camera constantly due to the game being top-down.  Two minor grievances with the game: - Can't pet the dog. - THE RAT.

text: I have over 100 hours and 100% achievements unlocked in Hades I. I never expected the 2nd game to exceed my expectations and take everything amazing about the first game and make it even better. Over 50 hours in the game before v1.0 and I feel like I still have so much to do, there is SO much content. The way the game takes you through the content whilst telling its great story and incrementally making your character stronger is top tier design. Every death feels like I learnt something and always want to build on it to take on the next big boss. It honestly feels like this game has twice as much content and replay-ability as Hades I did, and I am excited to continue my journey through the rest of the game, making my character stronger and improving my gear. I'm not sure what they have planned for v1.0 release but I honestly can't wait and I'm sure it will be amazing and they keep building on it.

text: Masssive kudos to Supergiant for delivering another brilliant entry into their line of incredible games. I really wasn't expecting all that much from a sequel to a [b]roguelike[/b] of all genres, and I especially wasn't expecting Hades 2 to top the masterpiece that was its predecessor.  Somehow, Supergiant has managed to deliver the same visually stylish, slick, and punchy combat from the first game, but elevated it to levels I didn't think possible.  The wider variety of weapons, aspects, and boons on top of different zones made this a really fun experience. Progression also feels faster, which can take away some of that typical roguelike fatigue.  The only downsides are IMO, a weaker story and more of a grind to get the epilogue, but the rest of the game is so good that none of that really detracts from the overall game.  Definitely a recommended play, even for those who typically aren't into roguelikes. But do play the first game first as this is a direct sequel!

text: This review comes from someone who has gotten all of the Steam achievements for the first game.  From my perspective, it is a mechanical improvement in almost every way. The combat, and progression system is far more engaging, and that isn't to disrespect what was accomplished in the original. Super Giant have truly outdone themselves.  The game is not without its faults however, though these are largely preferential on my part.  I found the story to be less engaging than the first. It's still written excellently, (barring a few incongruities that I won't get into here) and has wonderfully realized characters with some of the best dialogue from this medium that I've ever had the pleasure of listening to.   My issue more so comes from the premise. I much preferred the original's familial drama, and how Zagreus worked though it by doing battle with his father, over and over again. It's quite a novel concept. Having a plot that revolves around saving the world is something that can be done effectively, but defeating the big bad starts to lose its luster after the tenth or so time you do it. I am well aware that it is justified within the narrative, but Chronos resurrecting after each fight makes him feel less like an ever present threat, and more like an annoying pest that just keeps showing up.

text: Hades II is more Hades, and that’s not a bad thing. But after a fantastic first stretch, the endgame drags, progression stops changing how you play, and the story doesn’t land the way the first game’s did. It feels more like a big expansion than a true sequel.  [h2]What works[/h2] All the high-quality presentation from the first game is back. It’s a fast-paced action roguelite with incredible voice acting, gorgeous art direction, and a simple but satisfying upgrade system. It takes Greek mythology and keeps finding interesting, modern twists on the classic tales.  Hades II also adds a lot. Combat leans more on synergies and spell usage than its predecessor, and there’s far more variety in enemies, weapons, and areas. Its progression can be really fun and feels much more natural compared to Hades, at least early on both the arcana system and the crafting systems allow for a more addicting and understandable gameplay loop compared to the first game. For the first 30 or so hours, it’s easy to recommend.  Lastly its an extremely well optimized game. I almost forgot to put this in my review because not once did I ever have problems with stutters, loading screens or any other performance issues. Especially in nowadays gaming landscape, its a breath of fresh air to have a game just work flawlessly.  [h2]The endgame grind[/h2] My biggest pet peeve is how slow and tedious the game becomes after the main story. Around 95% of rooms pose no real threat, so most of your time is spent spamming attacks to clear them as fast as possible. The genuinely hard content, the modified runs, ends up feeling more like a stat check than an expression of skill.  Finishing the late story beats and character relationships is worse. You spend hours running through levels hoping the right character, the right scenario, and the right line of dialogue all line up.  [h2]Progression that doesn’t change much[/h2] The crafting system starts off fun, with a steady stream of upgrades, but very few of them actually change how you play. I would have loved a couple more weapons or enemy modifiers that forced me to adapt. There are some interesting new weapons, but unlocking them takes a long time. As a result, the second half feels bland: the only consistent late-game reward is making your base slightly prettier, and that loses its appeal quickly.  [h2]Story and Melinoë[/h2] Zagreus was a refreshing character with a lot of different sides. Melinoë, by contrast, is so focused on her one goal that she becomes predictable, and because most of the new characters are genuinely interesting, she sticks out. Without spoiling anything, she doesn’t seem to change much as a person, and it rarely felt like the story’s events really mattered. I wanted more closure. Even the epilogue, which took me 30+ hours after the main story, didn’t give me a satisfying farewell to this great cast.  [h2]Verdict[/h2] This might sound like I hate Hades II. I don’t. Hades was an excellent game, and more of it isn’t a bad thing. I’m just disappointed by how little this feels like an evolution. I wish it had a more conclusive ending, or gameplay that grew more over time instead of stalling after the story ends. For its low price and the sheer amount of content, it’s an easy recommendation. I just wouldn’t recommend going for 100% completion.

text: I loved the first Hades - it was an incredibly personal story with great replayability and really enjoyable rogue-lite design. The tight gameplay loop, unforgettable characters and Darren Korb's soundtrack made every run feel meaningful and pushing the story further  Here's how I felt about the sequel:  - gameplay - it's an upgraded version of OG Hades, refining what already worked and adding meaningful depth - I really enjoyed it and actually prefer more than OG Hades now. Selene's mechanics, the emphasis on spells weapons (a dream for mage fans like myself), new companions and expanded boon variety create incredible synergy possibilities. With so many options, the base game feels easier, but that can be adjusted later for more challenge - music and sounds - Darren Korb has done it again. The soundtrack is phenomenal, don't have anything to say, 11/10 - visuals - it's Hades, but polished. The attention to detail in animations and art direction is impressive without overshadowing the foundation that made the original beautiful. Witch theme is also nuts - dialogues - well-written, you don't get tired over campaign + the voiceover also amazing  Not pros, but not cons either: - plot - This is where Hades 2 stumbles compared to the original. The story feels less personal, less intimate. OG Hades wrapped you in a tightly, human-scale narrative where Zagreus's desire for truth and connection drove everything forward. Hades 2 swaps that for grand, fate-deciding stakes and paradoxically, it makes the story feel smaller and more generic. The plot beats are predictable, mysteries are non-existent and you end up trudging through a predetermined sequence of events rather than uncovering something. It's serviceable, but it lacks the dramatic punch of what came before  - characters - Melinoe is well-developed with genuine depth and certain characters like Selene, Captain Schmemelus, Arachne and, ofc, Cerberus with Bouldy, are quite interesting. But honestly? Most of the cast feels like they're just... there. They hit familiar archetypes and typical story beats you'd find in every other game. There's little that makes them memorable or unique. Some character arcs even seem to just end right after the quest, without any epilogue for their story line. Compared to OG Hades' roster - where almost every character felt like someone you genuinely connected with - this cast feels generic by comparison. They're not bad, but I won't be thinking about them months from now  /// Despite the narrative weaknesses, I still love Hades 2 for what it gets right - I even completed 100% of achievements and had fun doing that. The enhanced gameplay, the mechanical depth and the quality of combat make it an exceptional rogue-lite experience. I'll absolutely replay it in future. Supergiant made a sequel that's more fun to play than the original, even if it's less compelling to experience  The original Hades set an impossibly high bar for storytelling in the genre. Hades 2 opts for bigger ambitions and broader strokes - and while that doesn't quite land narratively(IMHO), everything else is excellent enough to carry it through. [b]It's an almost perfect sequel, just in a different way than the original was perfect.[/b]

text: After clocking in over 40 hours in Hades II's early access, I can confidently say: this game delivers. It’s everything I loved about the original Hades—and somehow, it’s even more addictive, ambitious, and refined.  At its core, Hades II expands on the formula that made the first game a masterpiece. The combat is fast, fluid, and endlessly satisfying, with a whole new layer of depth thanks to fresh weapons, mechanics, and boons. The first couple of hours felt like learning to walk again—I was stumbling through the new systems, unfamiliar enemies, and pacing—but once it clicked, I couldn’t put it down. There’s a hypnotic rhythm to it: experimenting with builds, mastering new playstyles, and feeling yourself improve with every run.  Even in early access, the game feels rich and polished. The storytelling, voice acting, and art are already top-notch, and it’s clear Supergiant poured a ton of heart into every detail. The characters are compelling, the world is mysterious and mythic in all the right ways, and the loop of combat, progression, and discovery is as addictive as ever.  If you loved the first Hades, this sequel is a no-brainer. Highly recommended.

text: So I 100% both Hades games and I have a lot to say.   I want to start by saying I played this game since day 1 of EA and put over 150 hours into it before version 1.0 and enjoyed every second of that time. So if you want a short answer then yes I absolutely recommend this game if you like roguelikes or you want to try playing one. With that said let's delve into details.  [b]Gameplay:[/b] Honestly a big improvement from the Hades I. Gameplay feels more dynamic, weapons have more variety in the way they are played and feel, equipping a new weapon (or aspect) guarantees a change in your playstyle and build. And if you add the amount of new boons and gods you truly can never run the exact same build twice (even if sometimes you really want too). The change from multiple dashes into dash and sprint, addition of omega moves and overall more thought out moveset really break the, somewhat, monotonous mold of combat in Hades I, I really felt like I need to do more than cast-dash-hit-dash-hit-cast-repeat. Although there's still the thing of "optimal" builds where sometimes you want just one particular god or combination of boons on certain weapons and you have the means to get it in some capacity. But honestly I never felt like only one thing works and nothing else is worth trying. Plus Supergiant tried to solve this to some extent with new endgame keepsakes and I had a blast playing with them.  [b]Visuals:[/b] The art and animation in this game are godlike (pun intended). This is such a huge step up from the, already incredibly beautiful, Hades I. Now sprites have visual effects, animations and multiple art styles (when you get some hot springs cut scenes for example). Every weapon has a distinct animation (all the aspects also have slightly or not so slightly different animations) that changes with various boons you can get. Just incredible, nothing else to say.   [b]Audio:[/b] Music in this game sweeps me off my feet every time. It perfectly matches the mood of anything you do or go through. Not gonna lie I added a few songs from the game to my Spotify playlist that's just how good the music is. And I can't not mention my girl Scylla when I talk about music here, because on multiple occasions I found myself trying to draw out the boss fight just to listen to the songs.  [b]Difficulty:[/b] It's fairly difficult, especially with some vows and trials (great chaos above and below I'm looking at you). But the main story doesn't require you to do anything over the top and for me wasn't especially challenging.   [b]Bugs:[/b] So far I had only one issue on 1.0. Athena girl please I'm already trying to do great chaos below if you don't show up one more time when they give me your keepsake I'm gonna cry. And also I've seen that some people had trouble with some achievement requirements triggering but haven't encountered that on my own.   [b]Price:[/b] Absolutely worth the money  [b]Story:[/b] Now here's where it gets worse.  Hades II has a significant tone switch from the first game. Even though Hades I had it's very emotional and tense moments for the most part it was a light silly adventure with a heartwarming story about breaking cycles of abuse and reuniting the family. It wasn't the most brilliant or complex but it told you everything that you needed to know. And honestly when I rolled credits on Hades for the first time I was really touched by the events and finale. Now Hades II shifts into more serious high stakes kind of story. Now you play as basically a child soldier that needs to save her family. From the very first run you can feel how much more gloomy and serious it is. Although it's not a bad thing at all on the contrary it felt a lot more dynamic and every loss or win felt more meaningful. There are a lot of new characters and all of them are just *chefs kiss*. They all feel alive and real with their own flaws. The world really feels alive and well polished. And as I'm going to be much more negative just in a second I need to say that all the time I spent in early acess was magical and I'm jealous of people who can experience it for the first time. Now with that said... The finale was just unsatisfactory and felt rushed. With all the build up in marketing campaign with all the "Death to Chronos" slogans on every post by Supergiant it just felt like "wow that's the lamest ending that could've happened". And as a person who values story just as much as gameplay I had to put down the game for 2 days after I rolled credits and was contemplating if I even should 100% it. I finished my last achievements trying so hard to just not explore the post-ending story because it felt so unnatural. [spoiler] Honestly I was shocked that devs decided to take all the agency away from Meli and just let Zagreus, who we've seen like 5 times in this game up to this point, to decide what she should do with a man who caused her so much trauma and suffering. I feel like they wanted to give us the "same forgivness is the solution" type finale like in first game but it's so mismatched with the themes and tone of this game that it gave me whiplash from how much I hated the resolution.[/spoiler]  But to wrap up this already very long review. Do I recommend to buy this game? Absolutely. It was worth every dollar I've spent on it. Do I feel like the game is perfect? Not at all. But all in all it was a wonderful experience that I'm glad I had.
